articles.title: The Global Story - How porn changed the internet - and everything else - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: Tracking down the men who have made serious money from internet porn.
articles.body:
World Service , · 11 Nov 2026 , · 26 mins

Every day, tens of thousands of hours of pornographic content are uploaded to the internet. At peak times, 10% of internet traffic is people watching porn. But who is making money from it, and how? Journalist Patricia Nilsson of the Financial Times has spent the past six years absorbed in this industry - chasing down its money men. She speaks with The Global Story’s Tristan Redman about how they’ve changed not just the porn we watch online, but the entire internet. articles.body:
The UK has fallen silent for two minutes to mark Armistice Day on Wednesday, commemorating the end of World War One and to remember those who have died in conflicts.

Ceremonies took place at the Cenotaph memorial in London, the Royal British Legion National Remembrance Gardens in Staffordshire, and across the UK.

articles.title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
articles.summary: Some people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland can get help with heating costs during cold spells.
articles.body:
As temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments.

This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures.

In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets.

The average temperature in a local area must be recorded as, or forecast to be, 0C or below for seven days in a row.

The temperature is recorded by the relevant weather station for your postcode.

More than 1.4 million cold weather payments were made during winter 2025-26.

Who can get cold weather payments and how much are they worth?

To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.

Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including:

income-related employment and support allowance

universal credit - although there are certain exceptions

Each cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25.

More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.

The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year.

Hospital stays can affect your entitlement to the payment so you should tell the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus if you become an inpatient.

You should also update the relevant service if you have a baby, or if a child under five comes to live with you.

In Scotland, the winter heating payment is worth £62 , and is paid automatically between December and February.

Heating tips to keep your home warm when budgets are squeezed

How to keep babies warm in cold weather and other winter tips

How do I get cold weather payments and how long does it take?

You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments.

The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather.

If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service or Jobcentre Plus .

Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits.

They are separate to the winter fuel payment , which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances.

About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules.

articles.title: Caminhão cai em ribanceira de 50m de altura no Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: Motorista e passageiro do veículo ficaram presos às ferragens e foram resgatados.
articles.summary: Motorista e passageiro do veículo ficaram presos às ferragens e foram resgatados.
articles.body:
Um caminhão de mudanças caiu em uma ribanceira de aproximadamente 50 metros de altura na Serra dos Tucuns , em Crateús , no interior do Ceará, na manhã desta terça-feira (10).

O motorista e o passageiro do veículo ficaram presos às ferragens e foram resgatados em uma operação que mobilizou equipes do Corpo de Bombeiros e do Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu).

Os dois transportavam uma carga de mudanças procedente de São Paulo e faziam entregas em municípios cearenses durante a viagem.

No entanto, durante a passagem pela Serra dos Tucuns, o motorista perdeu o controle do veículo, capotou, e o caminhão despencou na ribanceira à margem da pista.

Motorista e passageiro do caminhão envolvido em acidente em Crateús foram resgatados em uma ação conjunta do Corpo de Bombeiros e Samu. — Foto: Corpo de Bombeiros/ Divulgação

Para alcançar as vítimas com segurança, os bombeiros utilizaram técnicas de resgate em altura e montaram um sistema de tirolesa para transportar equipamentos. Enquanto isso, os socorristas prepararam a descida até o local do acidente.

Para o trabalho de remoção das duas pessoas presas no veículo, a equipe utilizou equipamentos hidráulicos de resgate e removeu parte da estrutura da cabine, abrindo acesso aos feridos.

Após a retirada das ferragens, as vítimas receberam os primeiros atendimentos médicos ainda no local e depois foram levadas a um hospital da região. O estado de saúde dos feridos não foi informado.

articles.title: Cristão acusam intolerância religiosa em item do Enem sobre misoginia | G1
articles.standfirst: Publicações na internet afirmam que enunciado "generaliza e coloca a fé cristã sob uma perspectiva negativa". Tema chegou a ser discutido na Câmara Municipal de João Pessoa.
articles.summary: Publicações na internet afirmam que enunciado "generaliza e coloca a fé cristã sob uma perspectiva negativa". Tema chegou a ser discutido na Câmara Municipal de João Pessoa.
articles.body:
Uma questão do Enem 2026 que trata da misoginia em sermões religiosos da Idade Média tem repercutido desde a aplicação do exame em 8 de novembro. O enunciado apresenta um trecho de um texto do historiador francês Jean Delumeau e pede que o participante sinalize em quê está fundamentado o discurso sobre a mulher do qual trata o texto.

De acordo com a correção e o gabarito extraoficial feitos pelo Curso Anglo a pedido do g1 , a alternativa correta é a letra A, "concepções religiosas que remetiam à desordem moral." O gabarito oficial com a resposta definitiva ainda não foi divulgado.

Questão do Enem 2026 sobre misoginia. — Foto: Reprodução

A polêmica acerca da questão surgiu após pastores e influenciadores cristãos considerarem que a questão é enviesada e busca doutrinar os participantes ao associar o cristianismo à misoginia.

Em uma das publicações mais populares sobre o assunto, o pastor Issan Almada, que lidera a Projeto de Deus Nova Aurora, em Belford Roxo, no Rio de Janeiro, afirma que o enunciado "generaliza e coloca a fé cristã sob uma perspectiva negativa".

"O cristianismo não pode ser reduzido a uma caricatura de opressão e preconceito. A fé cristã tem uma história complexa, marcada também pela defesa da dignidade humana, do amor ao próximo e do valor da vida", ele continua.

Comentários em publicação do pastor Issan Almada sobre questão do Enem 2026. — Foto: Reprodução

Mas o tema não ficou só nas redes sociais. Em João Pessoa, na Paraíba, o vereador Carlão (PL) apresentou uma nota de repúdio ao Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep) por causa da questão.

Segundo o vereador, a questão "deturpa o cristianismo, remetendo a religião à desordem moral e gerando intolerância religiosa". Para ele, o responsável pela elaboração da questão foi baixo ao "utilizar-se de uma prova de conhecimento para poder denegrir a fé de um povo".

"A questão correta era marcar que o texto trazia concepções religiosas que remetiam à desordem moral. É isso que eles acham que faz a Igreja Católica: misoginia, preconceito, desordem moral. É isso que os que fazem a avaliação do Enem tentam colocar na cabeça da juventude e dos estudantes. Não cabe", disse Carlão.

Dias após a prova, o tema segue em discussão entre alguns círculos cristãos dentro e fora das redes sociais, e muitos pedem que a questão seja anulada por apresentar conceito que "generaliza o cristianismo" e "alimenta o ódio aos cristãos".

O g1 questionou o Inep sobre a possibilidade de anulação da questão, mas não teve resposta até a publicação da reportagem.

articles.title: Seca em Sergipe: 15 cidades estão em situação de emergência | G1
articles.standfirst: Para conter os impactos do desabastecimento, caminhões-pipa estão em operação nos municípios.
articles.summary: A seca em Sergipe afeta mais de 82 mil pessoas em 15 cidades em situação de emergência, que dependem de 210 caminhões-pipa para garantir o abastecimento de água.
articles.body:
Caminhão-pipa abastece caixa de água em Sergipe — Foto: Bruno César/Governo de Sergipe/Arquivo

Sergipe tem, atualmente, 15 municípios em situação de emergência em decorrência de seca ou estiagem [Veja lista abaixo] . Pedra Mole foi adicionado na lista nesta quarta-feira (11). Ao todo, 82.791 pessoas são afetadas.

Os municípios de Monte Alegre, Porto da Folha, Tomar do Geru e Pinhão aguardam a portaria de reconhecimento federal. Pedra Mole aguarda também o reconhecimento estadual.

Segundo a Defesa Civil Estadual, para conter os impactos do desabastecimento, 210 caminhões-pipa estão em operação nos municípios.

De acordo com a Defesa Civil Estadual, o planejamento estabelece 50 litros de água por habitante por dia como referência para o atendimento. O volume é utilizado como parâmetro para avaliar a situação das comunidades e identificar quando o abastecimento começa a atingir níveis de maior vulnerabilidade. Quando a disponibilidade fica entre 20 e 29,9 litros por pessoa/dia, a comunidade ou povoado passa a ser classificado em situação de alto risco. Abaixo de 20 litros por habitante/dia, o nível é considerado muito alto e demanda intervenção emergencial.

De acordo com o coordenador de Integração e Gestão de Recursos da Subsecretaria Estadual de Proteção e Defesa Civil (SPDEC), Edivaldo Santos Celestino Filho, os reconhecimentos e homologações são fundamentais para ampliar o atendimento à população afetada.

“Com o reconhecimento federal concedido pela Secretaria Nacional de Proteção e Defesa Civil, o município poderá solicitar sua inclusão na Operação Carro-Pipa Federal. Além do reconhecimento federal, a gestão municipal deve solicitar à SPDEC a homologação estadual da situação de emergência. Essa etapa é necessária para possibilitar, conforme a avaliação da necessidade e os critérios estabelecidos, a inclusão na Operação Carro-Pipa do Governo do Estado de Sergipe”, disse.

articles.title: Corguinho registra 19 casos de leishmaniose e intensifica ações rurais | G1
articles.standfirst: Ao g1, a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde informou que monitora os casos e prepara uma força-tarefa com distribuição de repelentes e orientações aos moradores. Todos os registros estão concentrados na zona rural do município.
articles.summary: A Secretaria de Saúde informou ao g1 que monitora os casos e prepara força-tarefa para distribuir repelentes e orientar moradores. Todos os registros estão na zona rural de Corguin
articles.body:
Casos de Leishmaniose em humanos são investigados em Corguinho (MS). — Foto: Secretaria de Saude de Corguinho

O município de Corguinho registrou 19 casos positivos de leishmaniose na zona rural do município. Segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Saúde, outras 18 pessoas tiveram resultados negativos e um caso segue em investigação.

Diante do aumento de casos da doença, transmitida pela picada do mosquito-palha infectado, a prefeitura prepara uma força-tarefa com distribuição de repelentes para famílias de baixa renda e orientações sobre limpeza de quintais e proteção contra o inseto.

Segundo o secretário municipal de Saúde, Alex Julião, os primeiros casos surgiram no fim do ano passado. Na época, os registros eram isolados e não causavam preocupação. Desde então, o número de pessoas infectadas aumentou, principalmente em comunidades próximas a áreas de mata.

De acordo com Julião, dois fatores podem estar relacionados aos casos: a chegada de pessoas já infectadas ao município e a exposição de moradores ao mosquito transmissor em áreas de mata.

O secretário relatou que a equipe de saúde identificou pessoas que chegaram à comunidade de Zigurats, já com sintomas da doença. Entre elas, uma mulher que apresentava um quadro mais grave e testou positivo após receber atendimento no município.

Outra preocupação é a proximidade de casas e escolas com áreas de mata. Segundo o secretário, o crescimento da população e a chegada de novos moradores aumentaram a ocupação de locais onde o mosquito-palha costuma ser encontrado.

O calor e as chuvas também preocupam a Secretaria de Saúde, pois podem favorecer a presença do mosquito transmissor.

A prefeitura chegou a solicitar a aplicação de inseticida por meio do fumacê. No entanto, segundo Julião, o Estado não autorizou a medida devido às características da transmissão na região e ao risco de atingir outros animais.

Com o aumento de casos, a prefeitura intensificou as ações de prevenção e acompanhamento dos moradores.

As ações incluem visitas às comunidades e orientações sobre limpeza dos quintais, retirada de folhas acumuladas e instalação de telas de proteção nas casas.

A Secretaria de Saúde também prepara uma mobilização para o dia 19, com orientações aos moradores sobre como evitar a doença. Segundo a prefeitura, a compra de repelentes para famílias de baixa renda já foi providenciada.

Equipes de saúde também têm realizado atendimentos em comunidades quilombolas, fazendas e na região de Zigurats.

Os atendimentos incluem consultas, coleta de material para exames e acompanhamento de pacientes com suspeita ou diagnóstico da doença. Quando necessário, os profissionais também solicitam exames complementares.

Os moradores também podem procurar atendimento nas unidades da Estratégia Saúde da Família (ESF) caso apresentem sintomas da doença.

A leishmaniose tegumentar americana é transmitida pela picada do mosquito-palha infectado. A doença pode causar feridas na pele e, em alguns casos, atingir o nariz e a boca.

A doença não é transmitida de uma pessoa para outra. A infecção ocorre pela picada do mosquito-palha infectado pelo parasita causador da leishmaniose.

A Secretaria Municipal de Saúde informou que continuará acompanhando os pacientes e realizando ações de prevenção nas comunidades rurais e quilombolas.

articles.title: Secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos se muda para base militar após ameaça do Irã, diz jornal | G1
articles.standfirst: Bessent lidera esforços dos EUA para aplicar sanções contra a economia iraniana. Em outubro, a inteligência americana alertou que Teerã 'aumentou substancialmente' ataques contra cidadãos.
articles.summary: Bessent lidera esforços dos EUA para aplicar sanções contra a economia iraniana. Em outubro, a inteligência americana alertou que Teerã 'aumentou substancialmente' ataques contra cidadãos.
articles.body:
O secretário do Tesouro dos EUA, Scott Bessent, no Fórum Econômico Mundial (WEF) em Davos, Suíça. (Arquivo) — Foto: Reuters

O secretário do Tesouro dos Estados Unidos , Scott Bessent , deixou sua casa na região de Washington e se mudou para uma base militar, após uma ameaça do Irã contra ele, informou o jornal "The New York Times".

Bessent lidera os esforços do governo americano para asfixiar a economia iraniana desde o início da guerra no Oriente Médio , com a adoção de uma série de sanções contra a República Islâmica e seus parceiros comerciais .

O chefe de inteligência dos Estados Unidos , Jay Clayton, advertiu em outubro que Teerã "aumentou substancialmente" os esforços para atacar americanos no Oriente Médio e além.

Os esforços incluem ataques contra funcionários e ex-funcionários do governo americano, como Bessent, segundo o New York Times, que cita três fontes a par do assunto.

Os planos iranianos contra funcionários americanos chegaram "a uma etapa mais avançada", segundo as fontes não identificadas, que não explicaram a gravidade das ameaças contra Bessent.

A AFP solicitou um comentário do Departamento do Tesouro, que não respondeu até o momento.

Washington ordenou em outubro que funcionários não essenciais e familiares deixassem a embaixada na Arábia Saudita, após a intensificação dos ataques dos houthis pró-Irã contra o reino rico em petróleo.

Ao mesmo tempo, as partes ampliam os esforços para tentar acabar com a guerra. O chefe da diplomacia americana, Marco Rubio , afirmou na semana passada que a pressão econômica dos Estados Unidos contra o Irã torna desnecessários novos ataques .

articles.title: Workers launch general strike across Spain over severe housing crisis
articles.summary: Workers in Spain went on a general strike, in a mass protest against the country’s housing affordability crisis a few weeks before a snap ⁠general election.
articles.body: Workers in Spain went on a general strike on Wednesday, setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in a mass protest against the country’s housing affordability crisis a few weeks before a snap ⁠general election. It is the first general strike in 14 years to be jointly backed by Spain’s two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, as well as other labour organizations and tenants’ associations angry about rising rents and evictions. “We won’t stop until we transform this country’s housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the rentier minority,” said Alicia del Rio, ⁠spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, as the strike began at ​midnight. Spain ⁠has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to the central bank. With fewer people able to afford a home, renting has increased sharply, ⁠putting pressure on that market. The average rental price of €1,176 ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7% of a young person’s average ​monthly salary ⁠in Spain, according to the Youth Council of ‌Spain. Early turnout strongest at ports, auto plants Plans for massive protest marches in the afternoon were threatened by two storms, dubbed Charles and Bruna, that led weather agency AEMET to issue alerts for 14 regions over strong winds, rough seas ‌and heavy rains. According to UGT and CCOO, early participation in the ‌strike reached 90% at ports and in the automotive sector, with “total stoppages” reported at factories including Volkswagen’s in Navarre and SEAT’s in Barcelona. The unions also put early turnout at 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection and 75% in the energy sector. They said participation was lower in healthcare and ⁠social services, at 38%, and at 35% in the postal service. Tensions flared at the start of the strike at Madrid’s Mercamadrid wholesale market, where about 1,000 protesters gathered. CCOO’s Madrid branch said on X that police fired pepper spray at pickets and arrested one of them, with 13 people requiring medical attention. A police spokesperson confirmed the arrest but not the use of pepper spray, although he said it was used to disperse a separate picket line in the Carabanchel district. Election gamble The strike follows weeks of demonstrations and encampments provoked by the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid. Those protests, ‌along with parliament’s rejection last month of government decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted ​Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an election for November 29. The government has largely blamed the ‌right-wing opposition running many regions and municipalities for rising rents ⁠and insufficient housing supply. Sanchez, whose Socialist Party lags in opinion polls, hopes to harness voter resentment over housing ⁠and shift the political narrative away from a series of corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. But union leaders ‌and many of the protesters have ​said they also hold the central government responsible for the housing ‌crisis, as well as for Spain’s second fatal train ​crash this year. On Tuesday, train drivers walked out to demand more investment in maintenance and safety, causing widespread travel disruption.

articles.title: Peruvian homecoming: Pope Leo returns to the country that shaped his path to the papacy
articles.summary: Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
articles.body: Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV. Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories will likely be front of mind among the public as they welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday. The pope’s visit to Peru, which will include visits to Lima, Cusco and Chiclayo, is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who is a Peruvian citizen and who knows the country in depth. A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis. His mission during the pandemic “I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic. Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator. “He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop. Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis. “He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added. Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths, according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus. In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants. On the front lines during natural disasters Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023. “We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN. Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country. “I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region. The Venezuelan migrant crisis The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions. Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking. “The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled. Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén. “His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN. Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society. Promoting spaces for listening, and speaking Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s. At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered. Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures. A pope made in Peru Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo. His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave. In the past, the election of an American pope was considered impossible, given that the College of Cardinals did not wish to associate the papacy with the dominant political and cultural power. However, the cardinals who voted for Cardinal Robert Prevost in the 2025 conclave did not see him simply as a candidate from the United States. His experience in Peru garnered broad consensus among the cardinals, who chose a bishop with roots in Latin America — someone who speaks Spanish fluently and is attuned to the concerns of the people of that continent. The pope’s visit to Peru will be an opportunity for the Peruvian people to welcome Padre Robert back to the adopted country that shaped him — and that he shaped deeply as well. Reverend John Lydon, a priest and member of the same Augustinian religious order to which the pope belongs, and who lived and worked with Prevost for a decade, told CNN: “I believe his dedication to the poor and his defense of human rights will continue to define his visit.”

articles.title: PATRICK K O’DONNELL: Revolution’s epic test showed strength of our Greatest Generation
articles.summary: Benedict Arnold's 350-mile Quebec expedition through Maine wilderness pushed Continental Army riflemen to the brink of starvation and despair.
articles.body: A wilderness trek marked by rushing waterfalls, gorgeous fall foliage and optimism in the fall of 1775 soon transformed into a brutal struggle with starvation, torture and despair. What started out in late September as a high-spirited but long journey from New England through the Maine wilderness to invade Canada soon became a brutal test of survival that pushed members of America’s Greatest Generation to the limits of human endurance. The Revolutionary War generation, America’s Greatest Generation, suffered untold struggles in their epic fight for the freedom and liberty that changed the world and that Americans still enjoy today. These ragtag colonists not only took on the greatest army and navy of their time. They also had to guard against sabotage from within by fellow Americans who did not favor independence from the Crown. Simultaneously, they faced violence from hostile Native Americans. And perhaps most deadly, they battled the ravages of nature and the American wilderness itself. All these elements came into play in Col. Benedict Arnold’s ill-fated attempt to move his army from New England across the beautiful but rugged wilderness of Maine to attack Quebec. Spearheading that effort were the Continental Army’s first special operators, the riflemen. An advance team of 11 scouts, clad in hunting shirts, carried heavily laden canoes as they bypassed falls and marked trails and places for the bateaux, or flat-bottomed boats, along the way for the following army. THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER The scout team was made up of members from the 1st Pennsylvania Rifle Regiment. They and their leader, 35-year-old Lancaster native Lt. Archibald Steele, had been handpicked by Arnold for the expedition. These riflemen were some of the best shots in Washington’s army. Many had been long hunters who lived and hunted beyond the Allegheny Mountains and often had to battle Native Americans. Their woodcraft, scouting abilities and expert marksmanship would allow them to pioneer many aspects of early American special operations. Now, their skills were being called upon to help mitigate the dangers inherent in trying to move an army through the wilderness. WE SHOULD TELL REAL AMERICAN ADVENTURE STORIES TO TEACH OUR BOYS ABOUT HEROES The full story of these remarkable riflemen and the role of the Pennsylvania Long Rifle in helping win the Revolutionary War can be found in my newest bestselling book, "Revolutionary Snipers: Washington’s Frontier Commandos Whose Marksmanship Forged A New Way of War and Helped Win the Revolution," the third book in a trilogy on the elite units of the war. This groundbreaking look at the Revolutionary War recounts the untold story of the Continental Army’s first soldiers in an immersive "Band of Brothers"-style narrative that puts the reader in the boots of these snipers who preceded today’s U.S. Army special operators. Long lines of men hauling boats over strips of land between waterways are inherently vulnerable to ambush. Arnold hoped the advance work of his Revolutionary sniper scouts could mitigate the risk. In good weather and water, the men could travel 25 miles a day or more. Canoes, lightweight marvels of Native American engineering, could be carried by the men with ease. Steele’s canoe held five men with their weapons, equipment and provisions, while the remaining scouts rowed the second canoe. The group would have to traverse several major rivers, lakes, ponds and mountains on their staggering 350-plus-mile journey over rugged but beautiful terrain. In contrast, the trailing army, over 1,000 strong, three battalions, one including two rifle companies, deployed more than 200 heavy, ungainly bateaux to traverse the rivers, ponds and lakes with the constant possible threat of Native American or British attack. The shallow-draft, flat-bottom craft measured approximately 22 feet in length, weighed hundreds of pounds and could carry about six men each as well as six hundred pounds of gear and supplies. These clunky boats, constructed from green wood nailed to oak beams by locals of questionable loyalties, would be one of the army’s many downfalls. The river water and exposure to the elements warped the green wood, compromising the seaworthiness of the craft. "The bateaux were so badly constructed that, whether in or out of them, we were wet. Could we have come within reach of the villains who constructed these crazy things, they would have fully experienced the effects of our vengeance." Necessary repairs caused costly delays. It was early October before the riflemen reached the Great Carry, a 12-mile stretch of land and water that included three ponds between the Kennebec River and the Dead River. Rain turned the first part of the Great Carry into a quagmire of muck. "We were often half leg deep in the mud, stumbling over old fallen logs, one leg sinking deeper in the mire than the other, then down goes a boat and carriers with it, a hearty laugh prevails." Despite being wet and coated in mud from head to toe, the men kept their sense of humor, and the collective pain and grueling test of human endurance built an élan. AMERICANS ONCE SURVIVED ON SQUIRREL PIE, WHISKEY AND HOMEMADE CHEESE AFTER BRITISH IMPORTS DRIED UP However, weeks in the wilderness began to take a toll. The men suffered from the elements, constant toil and drinking contaminated water. They began to run out of food. Dysentery started to ravage the ranks, and carrying the sick became an added burden. To preserve their meager provisions, Arnold put the men on half-rations, but over 100 miles of uninhabited wilderness remained. This groundbreaking look at the Revolutionary War recounts the untold story of the Continental Army’s first soldiers in an immersive "Band of Brothers"-style narrative that puts the reader in the boots of these snipers who preceded today’s U.S. Army Special Operators. Misery continued to plague the mission. For three days, it rained, and a gale-force wind struck the men’s camp along the bank of the Dead River. The muddy river rose eight feet, uprooting trees, flooding the army’s camp and spoiling their meager supplies. The water rose so high that it became nearly impossible to tell whether the men were traveling up the Dead River or one of the many streams that fed into it, which had become rivers themselves. In the rapids and swirling water, one bateau was wrecked and sank. A barrel filled with gold and silver coins, used to pay the men and to purchase supplies from the Canadians once they reached civilization, sank like a rock into the swirling torrent. Facing sick men, diminishing provisions, a missing fortune, the onset of snow and freezing temperatures and the ever-present threat of hostile Native Americans or a British ambush, Arnold ordered a council of war to assess the situation. Eventually, he ordered a picked company of fit men to advance and find rations for the starving army in French settlements in the Chaudière Valley, scores of miles away, while the sick returned. GEORGE WASHINGTON'S REMARKABLE PRAYER FOR AMERICA STILL RESONATES 250 YEARS LATER Pressing forward in freezing rain, the exhausted expedition camped for the night, and the next day the riflemen and the remaining members of the force awoke to several inches of snow on the ground. The men tramped through deep snow, often sinking into a bog, unable to determine what was solid ground under the snow. The starving men had been reduced to a pint of flour per day for the past two weeks, starvation rations. As the sick and exhausted survivors began dropping out of the march, Arnold acted decisively to save his men. Using birchbark canoes, he set out ahead of the army with Lt. Steele and a few Revolutionary snipers. THE '1776 DIET': WHAT AMERICANS REALLY ATE DURING THE NATION'S FOUNDING Within several days, these frontier commandos encountered an individual who told Arnold they would be in the settlements in three days and have provisions for the men in six. The American officer sent back word that the men were to abandon their bateaux, and officers should distribute the remainder of their meager rations as they were expecting them to be replaced soon. Like concentration camp inmates desperate for food, the riflemen eagerly wolfed down the rations — their first full meal in weeks. However, unbeknownst to many of them, the meal would be their last, as a wrong turn extended their journey longer than anticipated. Eventually, survivors of the grueling march did emerge in early November after being subjected to such brutal conditions that some resorted to eating their own pet dog and others roasting the leather of their shot pouches. Misery continued to plague the mission. For three days, it rained, and a gale-force wind struck the men’s camp along the bank of the Dead River. The muddy river rose eight feet, uprooting trees, flooding the army’s camp and spoiling their meager supplies. They "staggered about like ... drunken m[e]n" unable to stand without the support of their rifles. Despite the beauty of their surroundings, "Every object tended to dismay the heart, already too much oppressed. The light that shone upon it served but to render its dreary aspect more visible." Ravenous from their additional days of starvation, the withered troops quickly butchered one of the cattle. Some waited for the meat to cook, others didn’t. Starved men can kill themselves from excessive food intake. Tragically, many became sick, and several died a day or two later after finally reaching the end of their epic test of survival. articles.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient, starts countdown to Ebola-free declaration
articles.summary: Kenya discharged its last Ebola patient, officially beginning the 42-day countdown toward being declared Ebola-free.
articles.body: Kenya on Wednesday discharged its last Ebola patient, officially beginning the 42-day countdown toward being declared Ebola-free, even as the number of cases recorded in the wider region topped 11,000 since the outbreak began in May. The country recorded nine Ebola cases in October after the first patient traveled from Congo through Uganda, transmitting the virus to four family members and four healthcare workers. The first patient and his mother died of Ebola, while the other seven patients have fully recovered. The government had identified 135 contacts who had interacted with the first patient. Kenya now begins the 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, provided no new infections are recorded during that period. But while Kenya’s cases have now been discharged, elsewhere in the region the number of infections continues to climb. In Congo, the epicenter of the outbreak, 11,042 people have been infected and 5,387 have died, the government said Wednesday. The outbreak also spread to Uganda and Nigeria through individuals who traveled from Congo. Kenya’s Health Minister Aden Duale on Wednesday said the 42-day waiting period is twice the longest Ebola incubation period and would end on Dec. 23, but insisted that the country would continue with its prevention measures. The Ministry of Health had earlier expressed confidence that the outbreak was under control, noting that all confirmed cases were linked to the first patient’s contact list. This indicated that there had been no community transmission. Kenya has faced travel restrictions following the Ebola outbreak, with Saudi Arabia announcing an indefinite suspension of visas on Oct. 30. The decision affected hundreds of Kenyan workers traveling to the Gulf for employment, particularly as domestic and hotel workers. The Ministry of Health had urged Saudi Arabia to reconsider the travel restrictions, explaining that Kenya’s first Ebola case was imported and that all subsequent cases were traced to the initial patient’s contact list. The ministry said all contacts had been identified and traced in line with established outbreak-control guidelines. The current Ebola outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus and has been described as one of the worst outbreaks on record. Kenya tightened its border controls designating a specific gate at the country’s main airport for passengers traveling from 10 countries that have reported Ebola cases or border those that have active cases. Passengers are being screened using thermal technology and all new arrivals fill a health declaration form that provides their travel and health information.

articles.title: Gaza’s infrastructure collapse leaves residents defenceless against floods
articles.summary: Winter weather has continued to wreak havoc in Gaza, with flooding and strong winds.
articles.body:
Damage from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has worsened floods caused by heavy rain, which have submerged large areas of the enclave, local officials say.

A deep weather depression has exposed how the catastrophic deterioration of the Strip’s stormwater and sewage networks is causing thousands of tents to be flooded.

Gaza’s infrastructure has been severely damaged by waves of air raids and shelling since the start of the war in October 2023.

Ramadan Rabaa, a Palestinian shop owner, saw floodwaters sweep through his premises in western Gaza City, destroying large quantities of goods and inflicting heavy financial losses on his and his neighbours’ businesses.

When municipal crews arrived at the scene, they could do little to help due to a severe shortage of equipment and machinery.

Rabaa believes that if municipal authorities had sufficient resources, such as water suction trucks, pumps, and bulldozers, his losses could have been minimised, potentially saving his shop along with other businesses, homes and tents that have been inundated.

The rain has submerged or damaged 70,000 tents, affecting approximately 350,000 people, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. In some displacement camps, water levels reached nearly 1.5 metres.

The impact of the weather is compounded by wartime destruction, with the media office reporting that more than 700km of Gaza’s sewage network has been destroyed.

Within 12 hours of the storm, Gaza’s Civil Defence received more than 2,000 distress calls but could only respond to 218, because of fuel shortages and equipment breakdowns.

Due to the ongoing siege on Gaza and destruction caused by Israel’s war, Gaza City’s municipality currently relies on only one bulldozer, which often breaks down, and two water suction trucks. Most water and sewage pumps are out of service.

“The municipality lost about 85 percent of its fleet of vehicles and heavy equipment during the war, after the Israeli occupation destroyed more than 135 vehicles, mechanisms, and equipment, leaving it with only 15 percent of the total previous fleet,” Husni Muhanna, a spokesman for Gaza City municipality, told Al Jazeera.

“The remaining mechanisms are old and worn out, suffer frequent breakdowns, and require continuous maintenance to keep them operational and provide the minimum level of services to residents and the displaced, so the municipality is forced to seek help from whatever resources are available in the private sector.”

The destruction extends to the drainage networks.

“The occupation destroyed six sewage pumps out of eight in Gaza City, and the municipality has so far been unable to restart more than two pumps, leading to a decline in drainage capacity to about 20 percent at best,” Muhanna said.

This situation has been worsened by the destruction of the stormwater drainage network. Gaza City has lost about 2,800 of the 4,800 drains that existed before the war, heightening the risk of flooding during heavy rain.

Muhanna warned that the challenges in Gaza City are beyond the capacity of municipal crews, with about a million citizens and displaced people concentrated in an area covering less than one third of the city, while 85 percent of infrastructure is damaged.

To address the situation, the municipality and local institutions have prepared an emergency winter plan requiring $1.3m worth of materials and field equipment. But it depends entirely on the flow of funding and supplies, which is being hampered by Israeli restrictions on Gaza.

Jibril Kashko, a businessman from a family specialising in heavy equipment, told Al Jazeera that Gaza City Municipality requested his help during the recent storm, but was limited in the assistance he could provide due to broken equipment and a lack of operational resources.

“What owners of heavy equipment in Gaza face goes beyond usual breakdowns, as they have become unable to obtain the simplest operating supplies, from spare parts, oil and grease, to batteries,” Kashko said.

Ismail al-Thawabta, director general of the Government Media Office, said the enclave requires between 300,000 and 350,000 tents and reinforced plastic tarps, as well as caravans, to replace damaged shelters. Mobile homes which were supposed to enter Gaza as part of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement have been held up on the border.

Gaza also needs 1,000-1,500 water pumps, 300-500 heavy machines such as bulldozers and excavators, and generators to power essential services.

Al-Thawabta said that repeated displacement and the destruction of most homes in Gaza have left large numbers of residents lacking essential supplies to cope with the winter months.

He said 2.2 million winter clothing bags, 5 million heavy blankets, 2 million water and moisture-insulating sponge mattresses, and about 400,000 heaters are needed to help Palestinians in Gaza cope with the bad weather. But the aid entering Gaza remains at a fraction of what the enclave’s 2.3 million population needs, due to the Israeli restrictions.

articles.title: Workers across Spain stage first general strike in 14 years
articles.summary: Strike disrupts public transport and industries amid demands for housing reform ahead of November 29 elections.
articles.body:
Millions of workers across Spain are striking to demand government action over the country’s housing crisis, less than three weeks before a national election that could bring the far right to power.

The 24-hour walkout, which began at midnight on Wednesday, disrupted public transport and forced businesses, factories and shops to scale back operations or close entirely across the eurozone’s fourth-largest economy. It’s Spain’s first general strike in 14 years.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours, including roadblocks with burning tyres in Barcelona, the second-largest city in the country. There were also scuffles between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market on the outskirts of the capital, Madrid.

The two main unions that called the strike, UGT and CCOO, reported widespread participation in the early hours “with significant work stoppages in strategic sectors”, including 90 percent in the automotive and port sectors, according to a statement posted on social media.

The CEOE organisation, which represents business leaders, said in a statement that the impact varied by region and area of work, with a “low participation” in most sectors.

The UGT and CCOO unions called the strike following a wave of nationwide protests over access to housing, sparked by the eviction in September of Maricarmen Abascal , an 87-year-old Madrid pensioner who died several days later.

The demonstrations included a five-week occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, where hundreds of tents were pitched, sparking imitations in other cities.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled over the past 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.

Spain’s socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap election for November 29 after his minority government failed to secure parliamentary approval for a package of housing measures proposed in response to the protests.

“This is not a strike against anyone, but rather one in favour of a common response from all levels of government to a real problem, which is access to housing,” he said in an interview published Sunday in the daily newspaper La Vanguardia.

The strike has been rejected by business groups, which have described it as an election-related protest, and criticised by the conservative opposition Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox.

PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo warned that unions risked being linked to Sanchez “forever” if they went ahead with the strike in the run-up to the election.

Feijoo, whose party leads opinion polls, said going ahead with the strike was a “serious mistake” following a high-speed train collision last month in central Spain that killed 69 people.

Spain’s average gross monthly salary is about 2,460 euros, while renting a 50-square-metre apartment in Madrid cost an average of 1,170 euros a month in October, according to property portal Idealista.

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, and 98.7 percent of the average young person’s income, according to the Youth Council of Spain. It’s well above the 30 percent share commonly recommended by housing experts and public institutions.

articles.title: Armistice Day: Powys church's WWI love story tribute
articles.summary: How two strangers and love letters from Gunner Willie Webber to wife Gladys led to a unique act of remembrance.
articles.body:
"My darling girl, you are everything to me..."

Those words were written by Gunner Willie Webber to his wife Gladys from the battlefields of World War One.

The newly-weds, who were married at St Edward's Church in Knighton, Powys, in December 1917, had very little time together as Willie - a gunner with the Royal Garrison Artillery's 297th Siege Battery - was serving on the Western Front. He was killed just weeks before the Armistice in 1918.

More than a century later, Willie's letters have inspired an extraordinary act of remembrance by the community - thanks to the efforts of two strangers who refused to let the couple's love story be forgotten.

The bundle of 100 letters, dated from December 1917 to October 1918, chart a love story unfolding against the backdrop of war.

After briefly returning home injured and marrying Gladys in late 1917, Willie went back to the front line in France.

He sent his new wife pressed flowers and affectionate messages, signing off: "Your own true hubby & loving sweetheart. Willie."

Willie wrote regularly and his letters are filled with hopes and dreams for the future.

But the reunion he longed for never came.

Just four weeks before the Armistice, in October 1918, the young soldier was killed in an accident when his gun backfired. He was 25 years old.

The couple had no children, no direct descendants and, as time passed, nobody left to tell their story.

Their story could so easily have ended there. Instead, those letters triggered a remarkable act of remembrance more than a century later.

In 2025, the collection of love letters was put up for sale at an online auction.

Among those following the auction was Andy Garner, a mechanic from Norwich, who collects, transcribes and self-publishes wartime letters - ensuring the people in them are not lost to history.

When he came across Willie and Gladys' correspondence, he was determined to save it.

"Those letters just kept drawing me back," he said. "I'm adamant Willie was going, 'Come on Andy, you can do this'!'"

The auction price kept climbing, but - in the final seconds - Andy placed a winning bid of £351.51.

Later, reading through the complete collection, he found himself deeply moved by the couple's devotion and Willie's steadfast belief he would make it home.

"No matter what he's going through, their love shines through," said Andy.

"It's giving them both the hope to survive."

Though he could barely afford the money he had spent, Andy was determined to publish the transcripts.

Keith Budgen, the man who had sold the letters, decided he couldn't keep the auction money.

"I woke up the following morning and immediately contacted Andy," said Keith.

"I said, 'You can have the money back. It's the right thing to do.'

"I had been given the letters, and I just knew that Andy had to have them."

The pair bonded over the letters and came up with the idea to commemorate Willie, the fallen soldier, in Knighton - the place where he and Gladys had married.

What followed was a remarkable community effort.

Within just two-and-a-half weeks, supporters raised £1,600 for a memorial bench at St Edward's Church.

The church immediately embraced the project and a remembrance service was organised. Bell-ringers created a special tribute, a bugler volunteered to play, and members of the Royal British Legion lent their support.

"The fact that he wasn't commemorated on any cenotaph, either in the town where he was born or in Knighton, made it a fabulous idea," said Ian Ferguson, of the Royal British Legion.

Reverend Rachael Storer, of St Edward's Church, paid tribute to Andy's determination to share the couple's story.

"It all started with those letters that he bought at auction," she said.

”Ultimately, this is a story about love."

Lynn Scales, who wrote a special standard for the bell-ringers in memory of the couple said: "Sometimes we forget the sacrifice that some people have made for the defence of this country.

"Gunner Willie sounds like he was doomed to be forgotten - but not any more."

Andy's wife, Lex, wrote to the BBC because she wanted others to know about her husband's work.

"Once he spreads the word, other people come on board and they all want to help because they care," she said.

"It seems to have this really beautiful ripple effect.

"Willie and Gladys were just regular everyday people, and for someone to actually take that time to remember them, I think it's beautiful."

More than a century after Willie wrote those letters, he and Gladys have found a new community. Not through blood or family ties, but through an act of remembrance initiated by two strangers, who refused to let their story be forgotten.

articles.summary: Alina Habba Mildon has been terminated from her $50 million contract with Concord Partners, linked to banker Julio Herrera Velutini, following Donald Trump's criticism of the deal. Discover the implications and details of this high-profile dismissal.
articles.body: Alina Habba Mildon, a former personal lawyer to US President Donald Trump, has been dismissed from her $50 million contract with a company established by the family of Venezuelan banker Julio Herrera Velutini, months after Trump pardoned the billionaire.Concord Partners terminated Habba Mildon in a letter dated November 4, citing a “failure to perform duties”, according to documents obtained by The New York Times. A person familiar with the Herrera family told the newspaper that her attention appeared to shift away from the company after she began a relationship with Turkish investor Turhan Mildon earlier this year.Despite the termination, Habba Mildon will retain approximately $14.5 million that has already been received from the company. This includes $6.5 million in payments and an $8 million signing bonus, according to the report.Her four-year agreement had been valued at more than $50 million and included an annual payment of $10 million, in addition to various bonuses. The termination means she will no longer receive the remaining payments under the arrangement.The decision follows public criticism from Trump after details of the contract emerged in October. The president described the deal as “totally obnoxious and outrageous” and urged the Herrera family not to pay her.Speaking to reporters at a Halloween event at his Mar-a-Lago property in Florida, Trump said he had objected to the arrangement and questioned the amount involved.“I thought it was terrible,” Trump said. “I told her, and I said, ‘I don’t want her paid.’ I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that. And it was far too much.”Concord Partners was established in Florida in late 2025 by Isabela Herrera, the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini. The billionaire banker, who belongs to a prominent Venezuelan family, had faced federal bribery charges in Puerto Rico before receiving a presidential pardon from Trump on January 15 this year.The timing of Habba Mildon's contract had attracted scrutiny because she signed the agreement while serving in a senior government role. NYT previously reported that Mildon entered into the arrangement in late October 2025, when she was acting US attorney for New Jersey. She later resigned from that position on December 8 and was appointed a senior adviser to the attorney general on the same day. Her work with Concord began on January 1, 2026.Habba Mildon has denied that her employment arrangement had any connection to Herrera's pardon. She previously said she had not received money to secure clemency, had not discussed the matter with anyone at the White House or Justice Department, and had done no work to obtain a pardon for anyone.A person close to her told the NYT that she was planning to take legal action against the family.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russia and Ukraine agree to a large prisoner exchange as talks conclude with no major breakthrough
articles.summary: Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials began a second day of peace talks in Abu Dhabi resuming meetings which Kyiv and Washington depicted as constructive.
articles.body: Russia and Ukraine agreed a large exchange of prisoners of war, envoys said Wednesday as two days of U.S. mediated talks concluded, but they announced no major breakthrough on ending the conflict that began after Moscow’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago. Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement. U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington’s peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results. As well as postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles for negotiators are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement. The session was the first such meeting since February on Russia’s invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians. “One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow,” said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, after the talks in Abu Dhabi ended. Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv’s contingent, confirmed the planned exchange, though Medinsky noted that the agreement was “in principle.” Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Umerov said Kyiv’s delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks. Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks, but he said their current statements “don’t indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace.” Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine. Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps. Ukraine wants to make sure Moscow doesn’t invade again, and EU officials have declared that any discussions on Europe’s security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire. Many in Europe see the inclusion of Russia in those plans as a concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a top threat to its security. Russia has demanded that the alliance pull back its troops from its borders. Russia’s security concerns were discussed at the talks, Kushner said, adding that Moscow was told it needs to provide different de-escalation and proposals for them to be acceptable to Europe. “The reality is, is there’s no trust right now between the sides. And that’s to be expected after a conflict like this,” he said. The context of the negotiations has changed since the last meeting in February in Geneva. The Trump administration now has to reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. midterm elections, and they could demand more support for Ukraine. Also, Russia’s wartime economy is under heavy strain, and Ukraine is reeling from devastating aerial attacks on its power grid. The talks came against the backdrop of continued fighting on the front line, where little territory has changed hands this year. Both countries are battering each other with long-range missiles and drones. Three people died and 11 were injured after Russia launched a daytime attack on a market in the southern Odesa region, local authorities said. Residential buildings were damaged and emergency crews responded, said Oleh Kiper, head of the regional military administration. Overnight, Russia struck the southern Zaporizhzhia region and the eastern city of Kharkiv, wounding seven civilians and damaging property, Ukrainian officials said. Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 627 Ukrainian drones overnight,. 150 of them over the region around St. Petersburg, according to regional Gov. Alexander Drozdenko. The drones started a fire at the port of Ust-Luga, one of the main facilities for Russian oil exports, injuring three workers, he added. Meanwhile, the Indonesian Embassy in Kyiv was seeking consular access to an Indonesian national who was arrested, according to Yvonne Mewengkang, a spokesperson for the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. She said the Indonesian government is taking the case very seriously and also working to ensure the protection of its citizens. Ukrainian officials made no immediate comment.

articles.title: King Charles III Coast Path winter section gives access to seal spectacle
articles.summary: It is designed to protect pups at Donna Nook Nature Reserve, near Louth, during breeding season.
articles.body:
A new, seasonal coastal path has opened, combining a national trail with views of a popular grey seal pup spot on the Lincolnshire coast.

The winter route of the King Charles III England Coast Path winds its way through dunes at Donna Nook National Nature Reserve, near Louth.

It enables the path to be accessed throughout the round, while keeping access to the beach at Donna Nook restricted during seal pup season.

Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust said the path to the north of Donna Nook offers great opportunities to spot wildlife.

In Lincolnshire, the path stretches 124 miles (200km) between Sutton Bridge and Barton-upon-Humber.

The new winter route replaces the summer route, which closes on 31 October each year for the seal pup season.

Managed by Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust, Donna Nook covers more than six miles (10km) of coastline between Grainthorpe Haven and Saltfleet.

The council said the route had been carefully planned to "improve public access while protecting sensitive habitats" and that more than 90% of the county's coastline can be accessed along the route.

This includes saltmarshes, dunes, and important habitats for birds and other wildlife.

On Friday, Donna Nook reported 28 bulls, 147 cow and 10 pups were visible from the viewing area.

Last year saw a "significant decline" in seal pups born on the Lincolnshire coast, according to Lincolnshire Wildlife Trust.

The trust said it manages the nature reserve to "ensure the safety of the seals and visitors" and urges members of the public not to approach seals.

Visitors are encouraged to use the designated parking areas at Donna Nook.

articles.title: Missing sculpture returned with an apology and £100 charity donation
articles.summary: Police were investigating the suspected theft of the scrap metal bird from Eden Court Theatre in Inverness last month.
articles.body:
A sculpture which disappeared from an art exhibition in a suspected theft has been returned with an apology and £100 donation to a charity.

Police were called after the scrap metal bird made by artist Helen Denerley vanished from Eden Court Theatre in Inverness last month.

It was due to be sold following the exhibition for the Scottish Mental Health Arts Festival to help raise money for Centred.

The mental health charity said the bird had "found its way home" along with a note of apology and a "generous donation".

More stories from the Highlands and Islands

News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds

The sculpture has an estimated value of £850.

Alana Kotrys, marketing and fundraising executive for Centred, said: "When we first realised the bird was missing, we said that we didn't know the full story and wanted to approach the situation with kindness and understanding.

"We're really pleased that things have ended this way."

She added: "Thank you to whoever returned the bird and made the donation.

"Your kindness means a lot, and it's a lovely reminder that there's always room for understanding and a positive way forward."

Denerley, who is best known for her large metal giraffes sculptures on Leith Walk in Edinburgh, was also pleased by the outcome of the appeal for the return of the missing piece.

She said: "Everyone I have told about the bird's return has had such a positive reaction.

"Thank you to the person who returned it."

articles.title: Ladakh bans protests ahead of polls: Sonam Wangchuk warns of fresh agitation against elections
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Ladakh administration has prohibited political protests, dharnas, rallies and other forms of collective demonstrations in Leh and Kargil
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Ladakh administration has prohibited political protests, dharnas, rallies and other forms of collective demonstrations in Leh and Kargil during the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) for the upcoming local body elections, even as climate activist Sonam Wangchuk appealed to the Centre to intervene, warning of fresh agitation over the poll schedule.In a post on X on Wednesday, Wangchuk shared a video featuring leaders from Leh and Kargil, including the local MP, appealing to President Droupadi Murmu, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Union home minister Amit Shah and leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi to intervene. The appeal comes amid growing opposition to the proposed elections and demands for political safeguards in the Union Territory.Wangchuk said talks on the restoration of democracy had broken down and alleged that the administration was moving ahead with the elections despite concerns raised by people across Ladakh. He also questioned the timing of the polls, citing harsh winter conditions, snowfall and the seasonal migration of residents."In this video the leadership of Leh & Kargil including the Member of Parliament have come together to appeal to the honorable President, PM, HM & the LOP & fellow citizens of India to please intervene before we are forced to start peaceful but intense agitations to demonstrate our pain," he wrote.The activist also questioned the delay in the judicial inquiry commission report into the September 24 incidents in Leh, saying it had been a year since the violence. He alleged that the administration was moving quickly to conduct the elections while the report and discussions on democratic restoration remained unresolved.Meanwhile, the restriction on protests was announced through an order issued by chief electoral officer Rahul Sharma on Wednesday. It prohibits political parties, candidates, workers, supporters and others from organising or participating in dharnas, protests, demonstrations, sit-ins, hunger strikes and rallies within the municipal limits of Leh and Kargil while the MCC remains in force.The order said such activities could intimidate voters, disturb public order and affect the atmosphere required for free and fair elections. It was issued under Section 282 of the Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Act, 2000, read with the Jammu and Kashmir Municipal Committee (Election) Rules, 2003. District election officers and police authorities have been directed to ensure compliance, with violations inviting action under relevant laws."No political party, candidate, worker, supporter or any other person shall organise, hold, or participate in any dharna, protest, demonstration, sit-in, hunger strike, rally or any similar form of collective political activity within the municipal limits of the Municipal Committee, Leh and the Municipal Committee, Kargil, which is likely to impact the peaceful conduct of elections during the entire period the Model Code of Conduct remains in force," the order said as quoted by news agency PTI.Polling for the Leh and Kargil municipal committees and panchayats is scheduled for November 21, while elections to the eight Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDCs) are scheduled for December 4.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Thousands of hoax bomb alerts sent to schools in Italy, U.K. and Ireland
articles.summary: Schools across Italy were evacuated on Wednesday ⁠after around 6,300 of them received bomb warnings, the latest in a series of threats and cyberattacks around Europe against supermarkets, blood banks, air traffic and broadcasters.
articles.body: Schools across Italy were evacuated on Wednesday ⁠after around 6,300 of them received bomb warnings, the latest in a series of threats and cyberattacks around Europe against supermarkets, blood banks, air traffic and broadcasters. Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland said many of their schools received a similar email threat from abroad but it was classed as a hoax and did not disrupt classes. In Italy, schools closed swiftly after ⁠the warnings, prompting many parents to drop what they were ​doing ⁠to collect children. “My daughter Dafne started crying because the kids did not understand what was happening, and she was still shaken when I picked her up,” said Nensi Bego, parent of a child ⁠at the Mazzini middle school in Rome. “This is so annoying. It’s obvious it’s just a hoax that disrupts ​lessons and ⁠disrupts everyone’s day.” A copy of the ‌message seen by Reuters also included a threat to target Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. She said the bomb alerts posed no danger and that police and other public bodies were monitoring the situation. “All students have been taken ‌to a safe area and remain under the supervision of teaching ‌staff,” one school in Rome informed parents through a messaging app. The email received in Italy was signed “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” according to a copy of the message seen by Reuters. “The (school) emails are public. (Sending the bomb alert messages) was as easy as drinking a ⁠glass of water,” a national security source told Reuters. The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent on Friday to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria. Russia and Iran deny accusations Some European officials suspect Russia may be behind a campaign of disruption to everyday life in European nations supporting Ukraine after Moscow’s invasion. Russia denies that and accuses the West of a smear campaign. Iran is another suspect. France summoned Iran’s ambassador on Tuesday after accusing Tehran of a cyberattack that disabled refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets last week. Iran rejected those accusations as “baseless and hostile”. Italian ‌Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said Wednesday’s threats were part of a clear strategy “to spread fear and ​create anxiety,” according to Adnkronos news agency. “It is not always the work of foreign countries ‌or hostile entities. There are also attention-seekers and lunatics ⁠who, at a time like this, cannot wait to unleash terror in a city or a region,” ⁠he added. Antonello Giannelli, head of the Italian School Principals Association, said the alerts were upsetting for students, families and school staff. “Even though today’s ‌threats are clearly hoaxes, we cannot underestimate ​the consequences of incidents that alarm entire school communities ‌and disrupt the normal conduct of educational activities,” he ​said.
