articles.title: A Kentucky father went to watch his younger son's baseball game against a team coached by his older son, then was escorted out by deputies; three years later, an appeals court revived part of his defamation lawsuit
articles.summary: A Kentucky father’s attempt to watch his younger son pitch against a team coached by his older son has turned into a years-long legal fight.
articles.body: A Kentucky father’s attempt to watch his younger son pitch against a team coached by his older son has turned into a years-long legal fight. According to the Kentucky Court of Appeals decision in John Carroll v. Charlotte Marshall, et al., available on Justia U.S. Law, John Carroll was escorted from a high school baseball game by sheriff’s deputies in April 2023 after a confrontation involving his elder son, a Shelby County assistant coach. Three years later, the appeals court has revived part of Carroll’s defamation lawsuit against the school’s former athletic director, while rejecting his other claims. Read more details about this incident here:A family divided at the ballparkThe dispute began during a two-game series between Shelby County High School and Martha Layne Collins High School. Carroll, a licensed Kentucky High School Athletic Association umpire and the designated umpire assignor for the 30th District, attended as a spectator rather than as an official. His younger son was a senior at Collins and the team’s starting pitcher, while his older son, Jonathan Carroll, served as an assistant coach for Shelby.The court’s account says that several adults connected with the games engaged in unsportsmanlike conduct, although witnesses gave sharply different versions of what happened. What was not disputed was that Jonathan Carroll was ejected from the second game and that John Carroll was removed from the premises by two sheriff’s deputies after a verbal altercation with his older son.For a parent, the situation was unusually painful. Carroll had gone to support one son, only to find himself at the center of a confrontation involving another son who was coaching the opposing team. The episode soon moved beyond the ballpark and into the school district’s communications with athletic officials.The email that started the lawsuitCharlotte Marshall, then Shelby County’s athletic director and activities coordinator, was coaching a softball game on a nearby field when she was called over to help manage the escalating situation. Afterward, she spoke with coaching staff, players and spectators before sending an email the next day to representatives of the Kentucky High School Athletic Association, a district activities coordinator and Shelby County High School’s principal.In that email, Marshall wrote that Carroll had previously officiated games between the two schools and attended games as a fan without incident. She said, however, that “lines were crossed” on April 12 and that Carroll had to be escorted out after a verbal altercation with the Shelby assistant coach, who was also his older son, as per the report.Marshall also stated that Shelby’s coaching staff did not question Carroll’s integrity or umpiring ability. But she said there were now concerns about his impartiality because he had allegedly provoked and taunted Shelby players, coaches and fans during the series.The email had immediate consequences. The KHSAA temporarily suspended Carroll from umpiring duties. Less than a month after the series, Carroll sued Marshall and the Shelby County School District, seeking an injunction that would lift a ban on his attendance at school sporting events and allow him to attend his son’s graduation.Why the defamation claim survivedCarroll’s lawsuit included two claims against Marshall in her individual capacity: defamation and tortious interference with a prospective business advantage. After the KHSAA investigated, Carroll was allowed to return to umpiring. He later interviewed for and received a promotion to 8th Region assigning secretary in July 2023.The Kentucky Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court’s dismissal of the tortious-interference claim. The judges reasoned that Carroll could not prove damages or causation because he ultimately received the assigning secretary position. The record showed that he was appointed as soon as the incumbent retired, only three months after Marshall’s email, meaning the message did not prevent the professional opportunity he sought.The defamation claim was different. The appeals court found that the trial court had applied the wrong legal framework when it dismissed that part of the case. Because Marshall was sued individually, the relevant protection was qualified official immunity, not official immunity, which applies when a public employee is sued in an official capacity.The court also said the trial court wrongly characterized Marshall’s decision to send the email as a ministerial act. Instead, the judges viewed it as a discretionary act carried out in good faith to fulfill her responsibilities for supervising athletic events and promoting sportsmanship. Because the legal standard matters to the outcome, the court reversed the summary judgment on defamation and sent the case back to Shelby Circuit Court for a proper analysis.What happens nextThe ruling does not mean Carroll has won his defamation case. It means the case will return to the trial court, where a judge must determine whether Marshall is entitled to qualified official immunity and whether the evidence supports Carroll’s allegations under the correct legal standard.The appeals court did affirm summary judgment for the Shelby County School District on the injunction claim. By the time the court considered the issue in October 2025, the 2022-2023 season was long over, making the requested relief moot. The court also found no evidence that the district had prevented Carroll from attending his son’s graduation.For Carroll, the decision keeps alive a claim tied to a highly personal moment: a father removed from a game involving both of his sons, then accused in an email of conduct that temporarily cost him his umpiring role. For Marshall, it means the legal fight is not over, even though the court rejected the business-interference claim and affirmed dismissal of the claims against the school district.A reminder about words and reputationsThe case illustrates how quickly a heated youth-sports dispute can become a reputation and employment issue. An email intended to inform athletic authorities about misconduct can carry serious consequences, particularly when it describes someone’s behavior, questions their impartiality and leads to a suspension from their work.It also shows why courts distinguish carefully between different types of legal immunity. A school employee acting in an official capacity may receive one form of protection, while the same person sued personally may face a different standard. In Carroll’s case, that distinction was enough to send the defamation claim back for another look.Three years after deputies escorted him from the field, Carroll’s central allegation remains unresolved. The Kentucky Court of Appeals has not decided whether Marshall defamed him, but it has decided that the lower court must examine the question using the right legal standard.You use AI every day. articles.title: What is northern Europe’s new drone and warship plan to counter Russia?
articles.summary: UK-led coalition of 10 Northern European nations announces joint defence framework amid rising threats from Moscow.
articles.body:
The United Kingdom has unveiled a plan to integrate the maritime defence capabilities of 10 countries, including the sharing of sea drones and warships, in response to what European countries see as a growing threat from Russia.

The Northern Navies Initiative is a British-led defence framework that will link the UK’s autonomous systems with its Baltic, Nordic and Dutch allies to create a unified surveillance capability to respond to growing maritime threats.

“The threats we face are multiplying … we must rise to the challenge before us,” First Sea Lord General Gwyn Jenkins said after the signing of the agreement on Tuesday.

“Together, we have shown what is possible when like-minded nations are united by a common purpose.”

The UK plans to spend 90 million pounds ($121m) on drones, sensors and artificial intelligence systems to help the Royal Navy counter Russian undersea threats in the North Atlantic and protect critical infrastructure.

According to Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow at the European think tank Bruegel, the new alliance is “a very important initiative”.

“No single Western European nation can credibly defend itself,” he told Al Jazeera.

So what is the new defence framework and will it deter Russian threats?

What did the UK say when announcing the plan?

Luke Pollard, the UK minister for defence readiness, introduced the new plan, saying that Russian naval activity around the country has increased by 41 percent in the first nine months of the year, The Guardian newspaper reported.

Pollard said the “huge increase” in violations justified the new initiative.

“The model that we want is where British autonomy [drones] can be teamed with a British warship or a Danish warship or a Norwegian warship and can hand that autonomy off to an allied nation’s warship,” the minister said, speaking at the navy’s International Sea Power conference held on the Prince of Wales aircraft carrier in Oslo.

Sailing the warship to Norway was “a really important deterrent signal that we stand ready to defend every single inch of NATO territory”, Pollard said.

The Northern Navies Initiative agreement will be a new network of autonomous systems equipped with advanced sensors that will create a unified surveillance capability to improve the detection and monitoring of submarine activity.

The 10-country alliance combines the UK’s Royal Navy with those of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) nations, a UK-led military partnership for crisis management in the High North, the North Atlantic, and the Baltic Sea regions. The JEF countries include Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden.

The agreement aims to support maritime deterrence and defence for the citizens of the JEF countries, allowing them to “act early, combine quickly and transition seamlessly into NATO command should the Alliance need to mobilise at scale,” the British Royal Navy said in a statement.

“In practice, greater interoperability means a Royal Navy frigate could transfer operational responsibility to another JEF member without losing momentum,” it added.

“One nation’s task group could direct allied sensors and uncrewed vessels, while a warship could repair, refuel and resupply in an allied port rather than returning home,” it said.

Future autonomous platforms will be able to plug in and out of each other’s command and control systems, “creating one large maritime force instead of 10 separate ones”, it added.

Analyst Wolff, of the Bruegel think tank, said greater interoperability was essential for better deterrence on the continent.

“Deepening interoperability among national navies, strengthening joint manoeuvres, ensuring clear command structures in case of crises is absolutely critical for credible deterrence,” he said.

“The deepening of cooperation is also necessary to [successfully] avert hybrid attacks, including against infrastructure such as deep-sea cables or renewable energy.”

While NATO provides the foundation for collective defence, the JEF initiative is aimed at bringing together “a smaller group of closely aligned navies together so they can work more closely, more routinely and at a higher state of readiness,” the Royal Navy said.

How significant are Russia’s maritime threats in the North Atlantic?

Western officials have warned that Russia has increased activity around subsea infrastructure.

In its statement about the new initiative, the Royal Navy said it was responding to “the growing threat posed by hostile activity below the threshold of armed conflict”, which includes “risks to critical undersea infrastructure, malicious seabed activity and other forms of hybrid aggression”.

In April, Britain said it had deployed military vessels to deter Russian submarines , which it said had spent more than a month in and around British waters, warning Moscow that any attempt to damage cables or pipelines would have “serious consequences”.

Pollard claimed that Russian spy ships, such as the Yantar, have been trying to obtain “an increased picture of our critical national infrastructure”, as well as “mapping our undersea cables”.

Russian frigates have been spotted escorting oil tankers and other trade vessels in UK waters, and in June, one fired shots at a yacht south of the Isle of Wight, The Guardian reported. A Russia-linked tanker, the Smyrtos, was seized following the incident.

As a result, oil tankers linked to Russia remain active but have been “sailing around the UK” to avoid coming through the English Channel, Pollard said.

Last month, UK officials called attention to the dwindling number of British frigates, which is expected to drop from 12 in 2021 to three by 2030, The Guardian said, and which could explain why the initiative was launched.

Pollard, the defence minister, blamed the opposition Conservatives for these shortfalls. “Now, because of the decisions taken 10, 15 years ago, we have fewer ships and fewer submarines than I would like available,” the minister said.

How has Russia responded to European accusations?

Russia has largely denied claims that it is posing a maritime threat to European countries.

Concerns about threats to undersea cables have particularly grown since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, Russia has repeatedly denied targeting them.

Most recently in April, the Russian embassy in London rejected the British government’s claims that its submarines posed a threat to undersea cables, Russia’s state news agency TASS reported.

Last year, the same embassy accused the British government of being “Russophobic” and “whipping up militaristic hysteria” after the UK accused it of directing lasers at British pilots sent to monitor the spy ship Yantar, in its waters.

“We are not interested in British underwater communications,” the Russian embassy said.

Moscow has accused the UK of carrying out the attack on the Nord Stream pipelines in 2022, for which Russia was initially blamed. Later German prosecutors alleged that Kyiv ordered the attack, which came months after Russian invasion of Ukraine. Two Ukrainian nationals have been arrested in connection with the sabotage. Their trial is under way.

Russia has also on occasion accused NATO of using fabricated threats to increase its military presence in the Baltic. Moscow has accused the US and its European allies of encircling it militarily through the expansion of NATO. It has opposed NATO membership for Ukraine as one of the conditions to end the nearly five years of war – Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.

articles.title: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
articles.summary: Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah is being tried on the charge of "publishing false news" and potentially faces imprisonment.
articles.body:
A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation.

Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge.

The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists".

Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left".

She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next."

Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.

Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down.

After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge.

At the opening session, Attalah's defence team requested the judge's recusal, arguing that he had "already formed a conviction in mind against the defendant", Mada Masr cited its lawyer Hassan al-Azhar as saying . The judge went into recess before adjourning proceedings for a week to allow the court to consider the defence's request, he added.

Mada Masr also said Attalah's appeal against last month's conviction was scheduled to take place on 25 November.

Egypt has largely stifled freedom of the press, ranking 169th out of 180 countries for press freedom, according to Reporters Without Borders' 2026 analysis. The group says that at least 26 journalists who were arrested in recent years remain in detention.

While most newspapers and television stations now keep to government lines, Mada Masr remained a rare, independent and investigative news source in Egypt. However, since 2017 the site could only be viewed from outside the country.

It had reported on alleged corruption and human rights abuses, and provided deep coverage of politics and economics, as well as regional upheaval and wars in Libya, Sudan and Gaza.

In her BBC interview on Sunday, Attalah insisted that the factual reporting and professional standards of Mada Masr had an important role to play in Egyptian society, which could benefit the government.

"It's much better if you have a little space left to have it open for professional media organisations who do rigorous reporting, because if we disappear, then you make the space for conspiracies and disinformation," she said.

"People need to know, people need to consume information and you're shooting yourself in the foot if you're killing the newsrooms that do it properly."

In September, six journalists with the independent fact-checking platform, Matsda2sh - constituting its entire newsroom - were arrested in home raids by the Egyptian authorities and held incommunicado for nearly a week.

They have since been charged with joining the Muslim Brotherhood and financing terrorism, and their lawyers report that several were beaten and electrocuted in detention. They say that no evidence has been presented linking them to the Brotherhood.

Egypt's former president Mohammed Morsi – who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood – was removed from power by the military, led by Abdul Fattah al-Sisi, in July 2013 after widespread protests. Under Sisi, who became president the following year, the Islamist movement was classed as a terrorist organisation, leading to a widespread clampdown.

On Tuesday, a spokesperson for the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, Thameen Al-Kheetan, called for the Matsda2sh reporters to be released, with all charges dropped.

He also said the case against Attalah "raises fresh concerns regarding due process and fair trial".

"We call on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information," Al-Kheetan said.

"The steps taken to suppress the continued work of both Matsda2sh and Mada Masr must be overturned. The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern."

Attalah has suggested the authorities might again be trying to silence independent voices at a time of economic strain in Egypt and regional instability.

It has been widely noted that recent legal action against journalists comes after the US State Department waived human rights conditions on $320m (£240m) in its foreign military funding for Egypt in September. This allowed the funds to be released as part of Washington's annual $1.3bn military aid package.

The BBC asked US Secretary of State Marco Rubio whether he had raised the recent crackdown on independent journalism with Egypt's Foreign Minister, Badr Abdelatty, at their meeting about regional tensions in Paris on Monday.

"We didn't discuss it today," Rubio said. "But… like anything else in foreign policy, there's always a balancing act to further the national interest of the United States. And in the end, Egypt has been a reliable and good defence partner of the United States."

"That doesn't mean you agree with everything another government does," he went on, adding that he was not "opining about their journalists".

articles.title: Jimmy Carter's family farm in Georgia has been acquired for conservation: Nearly 2,500 acres of fields and forest are set to join a wildlife area expanding to about 7,000 acres, with public access planned from 2027
articles.summary: The fields and forests where former US President Jimmy Carter spent his childhood, worked alongside his father and later escaped the pressures of public
articles.body: The fields and forests where former US President Jimmy Carter spent his childhood, worked alongside his father and later escaped the pressures of public life are set to become part of a much larger conservation landscape. The Conservation Fund announced on November 9 that it had acquired the Carter family farm, spanning approximately 2,458 acres near Plains, Georgia, with plans to protect it as wildlife habitat and eventually open it to the public. According to the organisation's announcement, the acquisition will expand the state's Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area to nearly 7,000 acres.The property, which remained closely connected to Carter throughout his life, was acquired for $8.5 million, The Washington Post reported. The Conservation Fund plans to transfer the land to Georgia's Department of Natural Resources in 2028, when it will become part of the neighbouring wildlife management area. However, visitors could gain access earlier, with hunting, fishing, birdwatching and other outdoor activities expected to be possible from as early as 2027.A family farm that shaped Carter's connection with natureThe land holds a special place in the Carter family's history. It was among the first properties the family acquired after moving to Plains in the early 1900s. Carter's father, James Earl Carter Sr, cultivated peanuts, corn and sugarcane there, and the future president spent much of his childhood working in the fields and exploring the surrounding woods and creeks. Carter returned to the property in 1953 after leaving the US Navy and taking over the family business following his father's death. Even after entering politics and eventually becoming the country's 39th president, he continued to visit the farm, finding time to walk through the woods, hunt turkeys and fish in its pond.His wife, Rosalynn Carter, and their children also shared a connection with the landscape. The former president and his wife often visited the property to walk and spend time outdoors, treating it as a place to escape the demands of public life.Carter's daughter, Amy Carter, recalled that her father continued returning to the farm until he was physically unable to walk around it. In his later years, he sometimes arranged for someone to drive him through the property. She told the newspaper that the Secret Service would often remain out of sight during his visits so he could experience a sense of solitude.The family has welcomed the conservation group's acquisition. Carter's grandson, Jason Carter, described the property as more than a farm, calling it home and a place his grandparents treasured. He said the family was grateful that the land would be protected for future generations.The property matters for wildlifeThe acquisition is expected to strengthen conservation efforts in a region known for its longleaf pine ecosystems and diverse wildlife. Much of the Carter property is wooded, although it also contains historic farmland and open fields. Its creeks feed into the Flint River watershed, adding to the ecological importance of the landscape. One of the most significant features is its longleaf pine habitat. These forests once covered large parts of the southeastern United States but have declined substantially because of development, logging and changes in land use.According to The Conservation Fund, Carter had requested that the property be restored to its native condition. At his request, the family retained a stand of mature longleaf pines, and one of his final land-management decisions involved replanting much of the property with young longleaf pine trees. The restored habitat also makes the land a natural extension of the nearby Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area. The Conservation Fund helped Georgia establish the existing wildlife area in 2019, with a focus on protecting longleaf pine habitat and threatened gopher tortoises.The gopher tortoise is considered a keystone species because its underground burrows provide shelter to numerous other animals. Protecting its habitat can therefore benefit a wider range of wildlife. The Conservation Fund said the newly acquired property is important habitat for the threatened tortoise, while creeks adjacent to the land support rare freshwater mussels. The wider landscape also supports birds and other wildlife, making the proposed expansion significant for both habitat protection and outdoor recreation.Public access planned before transfer to the stateThe Conservation Fund's plan involves opening the property to visitors even before the formal transfer to Georgia's Department of Natural Resources. The organisation expects public access for hunting, fishing and other outdoor activities as early as 2027. WABE reported that an interim lease is being planned to allow the wildlife management area to open the additional acreage by around mid-2027.The transfer to state ownership is expected to follow in 2028, after which the property will become part of the Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area. The combined protected landscape will cover nearly 7,000 acres, creating a larger space for wildlife and public recreation.The acquisition is also distinct from the nearby Jimmy Carter National Historical Park, which is managed by the National Park Service and includes the house where Carter spent his childhood. The newly acquired property is the broader working farmland where he grew up, worked and returned throughout his life.A conservation legacy beyond the White HouseCarter's connection with the Georgia landscape was reflected in his environmental record as governor and president. In December 1980, he signed the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act, protecting more than 104 million acres and marking the largest expansion of protected public lands in US history. He also established 39 units of the National Park System, including the Martin Luther King Jr National Historic Site and the Chattahoochee River National Recreation Area in Atlanta. His environmental initiatives included supporting the protection of wilderness areas and installing solar panels on the White House roof.Carter died in December 2024 at the age of 100. The preservation of the family farm now offers a way to connect that national conservation record with the landscape where his relationship with nature began.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Our neighbours are gone’: Gaza survivors recount horrors of deadly floods
articles.summary: A deadly sandbank collapse buried families alive in Deir el-Balah, as survivors describe desperate rescue attempts.
articles.body:
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Gaza is dealing with the cleanup of catastrophic flooding after storms submerged displacement camps and war-destroyed cities.

Heavy rain has directly affected 106,000 people in Gaza, according to UNICEF, with thousands of tents for displaced Palestinians submerged under water and latrines overflowing into camps.

The floods also brought death: a sandbank under pressure from heavy rain collapsed at the Ard al-Ribat displacement camp in Deir el-Balah, central Gaza, on Sunday evening, killing three children and a woman.

Without excavation equipment, residents had to dig through the sand with their bare hands to reach people trapped under debris. When darkness came, they used flashlights on their mobile phones to search for survivors.

Zahira al-Sahar, 58, was preparing to sleep in her tent in the camp on Sunday when she and her 28-year-old daughter were almost entombed in the collapse.

“I was lying in my bedding when something suddenly pushed me and came down on top of me,” al-Sahar told Al Jazeera. “The sand reached up to my neck. My daughter was beside me, and she was almost completely buried.”

Her sons came to the rescue. “I told them: ‘Pull your sister out first, then come back for me.’ They pulled her out, then came back and rescued me,” she said.

Meanwhile, in a neighbouring tent, members of the al-Nabhan family were also buried in the sandbank’s collapse.

“[When I realised] I started screaming and calling for people to come and help,” al-Sahar said. “I told everyone that our neighbours had been buried. We kept shouting: ‘Please, save them. Our neighbours are gone.’”

But the family did not respond to the rescuers’ calls. Eight-year-old Salah, his six-year-old sister Maryam, and their mother, Tahrir, 36, who was five months pregnant, were among the dead. Their father, Ahmed, who was only recently released from Israeli detention, is the family’s sole survivor.

“[Ahmed al-Nabhan] and his wife had been very happy after he came out of prison. They were looking forward to having another child in a few months,” said Suhaib Abu Darabi, 32, who was among neighbours who rushed to the site to help save them.

Abu Darabi said the collapse sounded like an explosion and was followed by screaming. The site was exposed to the elements and on unstable ground and collapsed after just a few minutes of rain. By the time neighbours reached the area, they found two tents completely buried under debris.

Abu Darabi said residents were digging with whatever tools they could find.

“We managed to clear some of the rubble, but we could not save the people trapped underneath. The scale of the collapse was far beyond what the residents here could handle, given the lack of resources,” Abu Darabi told Al Jazeera.

“The tents that collapsed beneath the embankment are what the world saw. But what people did not see was that all these tents fell to the ground that night. Residents had to repair whatever they could so they could continue living in them.”

In the neighbouring al-Zein family’s tent, four-year-old Habiba was killed, while her mother, Reem, and brother Ibrahim remain in intensive care.

The scale of the damage caused by this winter’s first storm, which began on November 6, was significant and has exposed the dangers faced by families living in tents with little protection from extreme weather.

This is the fourth winter since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began, in October 2023, and hundreds of thousands of people are living in tattered tents or makeshift shelters that have been exposed to the elements for years.

More than 26,000 households had reported damage to their shelters or other belongings by November 8, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported. The UN estimated that about 1.4 million people, or 65 percent of Gaza’s population, were living in tents or makeshift shelters when the storms hit.

The danger is only compounded by the extensive destruction of Gaza’s infrastructure from Israeli strikes. Drainage networks have been severely damaged, roads and access routes remain in poor condition, and municipalities lack sufficient equipment to remove accumulated rainwater and respond to emergencies.

Gaza’s Government Media Office described the Deir el-Balah sandbank collapse as a humanitarian disaster.

It said it held Israel, the United States administration and the international community responsible and the blocking of proper shelters, construction materials, mobile homes, fuel and spare parts was a factor in the deadly floods.

The media office also said the failure of the so-called Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza to act in the crisis also raised “serious questions about the purpose of these bodies”, which have been accused of working with Israel to continue its siege on Gaza.

The Board of Peace said in a statement this week that it had urged Israel to allow essential supplies such as temporary shelters and drainage equipment to enter the enclave.

Aid organisations have also repeatedly called for the entry of shelter materials and equipment needed to repair damaged tents and infrastructure to avoid a repeat of this past week’s deadly events.

Shaima al-Daour, 22, a displaced woman from northern Gaza who works as a nurse in the Ard al-Ribat camp, was also among those who rushed to help the injured.

“I tried to resuscitate a young child who was pulled out from under the rubble, but he had internal bleeding. I tried, but there was no response,” she said.

Al-Daour said another boy, aged 15, was brought to her with difficulty breathing. She opened his airway and he began to breathe, but his pulse was weak. With no ambulance readily available, she called on people around her to find any means of transport to get him to the hospital.

“I was surrounded by men, shouting at them: ‘Does anyone have a tuk-tuk? A cart? Anything to carry him?’ What I saw was unbearable. I could not save the little child in front of me,” she said.

“We need shelter and land where people can live safely. We also need equipment so that, God forbid, if something happens again, there is something available to help us.”

Al-Daour said she is still in shock by what she witnessed and is terrified by the prospect of the impending winter.

“I still cannot get over what happened,” she said. “Have the people of Gaza not experienced every possible way of dying? Have some compassion for us. Just have some compassion for us, people of the world,” she said.

articles.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
articles.summary: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
articles.body:
Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.

Demonstrations have taken place across the country, including in Madrid and Barcelona, where tens of thousands marched in the evening.

Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.

The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."

However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.

Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.

The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056).

That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.

Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.

Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.

And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.

"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.

Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests

The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.

PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.

Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."

Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.

Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.

The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.

Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.

"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."

He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."

With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".

However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.

"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.

Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.

Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

articles.title: Rubio backs blockade, Vance wants deal: Is Trump’s team split on Iran war?
articles.summary: Torn between military action and diplomacy, US appears to settle for drawn-out economic pressure campaign, blockade.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said that Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran is proving so effective that a resumption of large-scale military operations is unnecessary.

His remarks are the latest in an often-evolving series of messages from US President Donald Trump’s administration on the conflict with Iran. They also come after a crushing midterm defeat for Trump’s Republican Party, which the president acknowledged was likely partly driven by public opposition to the war.

So how do Rubio’s latest remarks compare with the positions of other administration officials, and what do they say about the state of the conflict?

What have Trump, Rubio and Vance said about the conflict?

Rubio made his latest comments on Tuesday after meeting with foreign ministers from the Group of Seven (G7) forum in Paris.

He said he told G7 allies that “the economic campaign [against Iran] is so devastating that right now there is no need for major combat operations”.

“We don’t need to conduct military strikes if we’re achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure. That’s not stalemate,” Rubio said.

“The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.

Rubio also pushed G7 allies to help “protect shipping” around the embattled Strait of Hormuz, where he said US forces would stay.

The secretary of state’s remarks were largely in line with Trump’s comments on Monday, when the president said further strikes against Iran were “quite unlikely”.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the US’s Gulf allies preferred a continuation of the “status quo”, referring to the US’s blockade of Iranian ports. Trump added that there appears to be “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict, but that the US remains “locked and loaded” should circumstances change.

Vice President JD Vance, who has been more critical of the war and recently wrote a lengthy social media post blaming the Republican Party’s midterm defeat on the conflict, favours a deal with Iran, which Trump does not believe is possible right now, the Reuters news agency cited an informed source as saying.

Between sanctions and diplomacy: What are the divisions on Iran war strategy?

Negotiations to end the US-Iran conflict have been largely stalled for months, as Iran continues to target vessels it claims are violating its conditions for transit through the Strait of Hormuz and the US ramps up sanctions against Iran and continues to blockade Iranian ports, with plans to block Iran’s land-based supply routes as well.

Back in September, Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks. Tehran has since said that timeline could be brought down to two days . Tehran’s demands for the US include lifting sanctions Washington imposed after the collapse of a June memorandum of understanding (MoU), reducing the US military presence in the region, reinstating oil waivers and releasing frozen Iranian funds.

Trump, torn between restarting an unpopular war or pushing harder for a deal with Tehran, has for now settled on a middle ground: doubling down on the pressure campaign against Iran while avoiding a return to full-scale military action, according to officials quoted by Axios.

That strategy is backed by several key administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and CIA Director John Ratcliffe, as well as Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, Axios cited US officials as saying.

However, several US allies in the region, including Pakistan, Iraq and Turkiye, are concerned that a drawn-out US pressure campaign against Iran could hurt their own business interests, said one official cited by the news outlet.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said that a long-term US policy of intensive sanctions and a blockade against Iran would only prolong an “unstable status quo” that would eventually escalate into more military confrontation.

However, he said one “walk-away” option for Trump could be to quietly relax the sanctions and blockade while maintaining them “on paper”.

In this case, “Trump walks away and claims to retain the blockade and sanctions infrastructure, but in reality, allows it to imperceptibly wither away,” Parsi told Al Jazeera. “The blockade begins to loosen, sanctions enforcement begins to decay, and slowly but surely, Asian and Middle Eastern countries begin trading with and investing in Iran.”

“A new equilibrium emerges in which sanctions enforcement is strong enough for the US to claim the restrictions are still in place, yet weak enough to prevent Tehran from challenging the new status quo,” Parsi said.

Have the midterm election results impacted Trump’s strategy?

Negar Mortazavi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, DC, said the Republicans’ resounding election defeat “dramatically raised the political cost of more escalation” and gave the Democrats a stronger mandate to challenge the war.

“If Democrats unite and use their new power aggressively, they can make it increasingly difficult for Trump to continue the war, pressuring him to end it,” Mortazavi told Al Jazeera.

“A diplomatic breakthrough is not guaranteed, but the political and strategic costs of escalation keep growing, making another round of war less likely,” she added.

Both Trump and Vance have acknowledged that the Iran war was partly to blame for the Republicans’ loss, with Trump saying voters were not ready for petrol prices to rise.

According to a poll by Reuters/Ipsos completed on Monday, 71 percent of Americans – including 93 percent of Democrats and 51 percent of Republicans – favour congressional legislation that would halt the Iran war.

Iranian officials have upped their rhetoric even as Washington appears to be moving away from military escalation.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Tuesday said the war will “not end either through military means or by increasing sanctions”, but only through “using the language of respect”.

In comments carried by Iran’s IRNA news agency, he urged the US “to act on Iran’s demands and conditions”, adding that Trump “should have realised much earlier that he has not achieved, and will not achieve, any of his goals in the war with Iran”.

Iran’s top security chief Mohsen Rezaei, in a social media post on Monday, said the US government had been “wrecked” by the war and that it was time for it to “surrender” to Iran’s demands.

Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran, noted that Iran’s language has become “more confident than ever before”.

“They’re trying to convey to the public, internally, and also to the Americans, that there is no way this war can be declared over without responding to those conditions presented by Iran during the negotiations,” said Vall.

What is the current status of diplomacy?

The Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Tuesday said that Doha is “working tirelessly” in its ongoing mediation efforts, and has received positive reactions from both sides.

Trump, the day before, after hosting Qatar’s prime minister at the White House , also spoke of “momentum towards the end of this conflict”, adding that “Iran is talking to us, and they’re talking very politely”.

Rubio, for his part, said the US remains “open to diplomacy”, but called Iran’s current demands “totally unrealistic”.

“We expect that could change – and if it does, we’re prepared for diplomacy,” he said.

Iranian officials, meanwhile, have appeared more sceptical of the latest reports of mediation, insisting that the US must accept their demands.

Rezaei on Tuesday said there ⁠were no negotiations taking place between Tehran and Washington and that Iran would retaliate against any new US attack by targeting US bases “far away”. He also said Iran would not let any of its enriched nuclear material leave the country, ruling out a concession the US has sought in potential nuclear talks.

In a social media post, Rezaei went on to accuse the US of “manufacturing FAKE NEWS about imaginary talks”.

articles.title: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of iconic NYC gourmet food shop, dies at 94
articles.summary: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of the famed New York City gourmet food shop, has died.
articles.body: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of the famed New York City gourmet food shop, has died. He was 94. Zabar’s announced his death in a post on its Instagram on Tuesday, calling Stanley Zabar “a quiet force behind our family business.” According to the post, Zabar worked alongside his brother, Saul Zabar, “to build upon and carry forward the vision of their parents, Louis and Lillian Zabar.” Louis and Lillian Zabar opened the eatery on Manhattan’s Upper West Side in 1934. The cause of death was not announced, but The New York Times reported that Zabar died from cancer, citing his daughter Dr. Sondra Zabar. According to the Instagram post, Zabar worked behind the scenes at the world-renowned shop, and his “legal and financial acumen was vital in shaping Zabar’s into a beloved New York City institution.” According to the Times, Zabar handled the business side of the store but often appeared to greet customers. Saul Zabar, on the other hand, oversaw the store’s operations, taste-testing its famous smoked fish and coffee. A third partner, Murray Klein, did the store’s marketing, it reported. Zabar and his wife, Judith Zabar, were also philanthropists, the store said in the post. The couple “dedicated their time and resources to the arts, education and culinary training,” it said, adding that they supported Hunter College, the New York Public Library, Symphony Space, NYU Langone Health and the Careers through Culinary Arts Program. But above all else, “Stanley’s greatest devotion was to his family,” the Instagram post said. Zabar was a lifelong New Yorker, and he and his wife raised their family on the Upper West Side, “deeply embedded in the neighborhood that generations of Zabars have called home.” “He will be remembered for the business he helped build, the countless opportunities he created for others and his unwavering dedication to his family and community,” the store wrote. The food emporium has been a staple of uptown Manhattan for nearly 100 years, maintaining its presence on 80th Street and Broadway since its opening in the 1930s. According to a blurb on the shop’s website by Saul and Stanley Zabar, quality was of the utmost importance to its founders. The store said it introduced New Yorkers to brie in the 1960s and to sun-dried tomatoes and gnocchi in the 1970s. In the 1980s, “we got so excited about caviar — and wanted everyone to taste it — that our prices set off a so-called ‘Caviar War,’” the food emporium said, and it won, according to the website. The business has since grown, and generations later, it remains in the family. “With our sons, daughters and their cousins, we’re still at it — hand-slicing meltingly delicious smoked fish behind our deli counter…offering tastes of the latest artisanal cheeses…setting out fresh-baked batches of rugelach (it’s our Bubbe’s recipe)…overseeing the roasting of our special coffee blends (we sell 400,000 pounds a year!)” the store said on its website. “Retire? Not on your life — we’re having too much fun!”

articles.title: 'Why should daily commutes become longer?': PM Modi welcomes Noida Aqua Line extension to Greater Noida Sector 4, a Rs 2,390 crore elevated corridor with 5 new stations
articles.summary: NOIDA: “As Noida and Greater Noida grow, why should daily commutes become longer?” Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Wednesday as he welcomed the Union
articles.body: NOIDA: “As Noida and Greater Noida grow, why should daily commutes become longer?” Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Wednesday as he welcomed the Union Cabinet's approval for extending the Aqua Line Metro corridor from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4.The expansion, he said, would improve access to offices, schools, hospitals and commercial hubs, reduce congestion and make daily travel easier for residents.In a post on X, Modi described the approval as a major boost to connectivity and ease of living in the two rapidly growing cities.The project will add an 8.449-km elevated stretch with five stations to the Noida Metro network and is expected to improve public transport access across several residential, commercial and institutional areas.Union minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the project would cost Rs 2,390 crore. Once operational, the extension will take the combined active Metro Rail network in Noida and Greater Noida to 71.878 km, according to the government.Five stations, one key interchangeThe approved corridor will run from Noida Sector 51 to Greater Noida Sector 4, adding approximately 8.449 km of elevated metro tracks and five stations.One of the key connectivity gains will be the interchange with the Blue Line at Noida Sector 61. This will allow commuters to connect with the Blue Line network and improve access to other parts of the Delhi-NCR region.Vaishnaw said the extension would benefit several IT companies and Global Capability Centres (GCCs) located in the area. He also pointed to the potential for better access to airports from different parts of the Delhi region.The minister said a major multimodal transportation hub, including a mega railway terminal, was also being developed at the site.The metro extension is expected to complement this infrastructure and improve access to transport hubs, including Delhi's airport, railway stations and bus depots.Commercial hubs set to get better connectivityThe extension is expected to link several commercial and business locations across Noida and Greater Noida with the metro network.Among the commercial destinations mentioned by the government are Gaur City Mall, H&S Mall, Blue Sapphire Mall and Anthurium Mall, along with commercial spaces in Greater Noida Sector 4. IKEA in Noida Sector 51 is also among the locations expected to benefit.The corridor will also improve access to offices and business establishments, including Tech Mahindra's office and TCL Tech's office in Noida Sector 60, the Oil Industry Development Board in Sector 73 and Golden I's office and commercial space in Greater Noida Sector 4.With several multinational companies and IT hubs located in these areas, the government expects the extension to make daily commutes easier for employees and other professionals travelling to work.A metro closer to homes, schools and hospitalsThe proposed stretch is also expected to improve connectivity for residents of major housing clusters in the region.The government has identified Cleo County Residences in Noida Sector 122 and Gaur City 1 and 2 in Greater Noida Sector 4 among the residential areas that will benefit from the expansion.Educational institutions in the corridor's catchment areas include Delhi Public School in Noida Sector 122.The improved network is also expected to provide better access to healthcare facilities such as Kailash Hospital, Rama Hospital in Noida Sector 70, Cloud9 Hospital in Sector 51 and Rama Hospital in Sector 62.By connecting residential areas with workplaces, educational institutions, hospitals and commercial centres, the extension is expected to serve commuters travelling for employment, business, education and other everyday needs.Less traffic, shorter journeysThe expansion is expected to provide an alternative to road transport and help ease congestion in Noida and Greater Noida. With more commuters using the metro, the government expects a reduction in road traffic, smoother movement of vehicles and shorter travel times.The addition of the new stretch is also expected to reduce carbon emissions compared with conventional fossil-fuel-based transport.Greater use of public transport could help lower dependence on private vehicles while improving access to different parts of the two cities.The government has also highlighted the project's potential to improve productivity by reducing commuting time and making workplaces and other destinations more accessible. Improved metro connectivity could also encourage local businesses and attract investment in areas that were previously less accessible.A boost to Noida's expanding metro networkThe 8.449-km extension will add to the existing metro infrastructure in Noida and Greater Noida, taking their combined active network to 71.878 km once the new corridor becomes operational.The government said the project would improve access to public transport across different socio-economic groups and help reduce disparities in connectivity.It is expected to make essential services and major destinations more accessible while supporting the region's continued urban and economic development.(With agency inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Noida | Silver Rate in Noida | Bank Holidays in Noida | Public Holidays in Noida | Noida AQI | Weather in Noida | Petrol Price in Noida | Diesel Price in Noida | CNG Price in Noida | LPG Price in NoidaStay updated with the latest Noida news. articles.title: Antonio Sabàto Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son arrested in connection with a fatal hit-and-run in Alaska
articles.summary: The son of Oscar-nominated actress Virginia Madsen and soap star Antonio Sabàto Jr.
articles.body: The son of Oscar-nominated actress Virginia Madsen and soap star Antonio Sabàto Jr. was arrested in connection with a fatal hit-and-run in Alaska, police said Tuesday. Jack Antonio Sabàto, 32, was booked into the Anchorage Correctional Complex on suspicion of leaving the scene of a deadly accident and failing to assist, jail records show. The crash happened a little before 5:48 a.m. local time Monday when officers and medics came to the aid of an “unresponsive adult male” at the intersection of Airport Heights Drive and Debarr Road, according to an Anchorage police statement. Carl Simmonds, a 42-year-old pedestrian, “had been struck by a vehicle, which then fled the scene,” police added. Simmonds was pronounced dead at the scene. Later in the day, police identified the younger Sabàto as the driver who was allegedly behind the wheel of Chevrolet Tahoe, officials said. On the screen, the elder Sabàto, 54, is best known for his work on “General Hospital” from 1992 to 1995 and “Melrose Place” in 1995. In recent years, he has become an outspoken supporter of President Donald Trump — a political stance the actor claims has damaged his career in Hollywood. He addressed the Republican National Convention in 2016 on the same night as fellow Hollywood conservative Scott Baio. “That’s (Trump) the only choice, there is no one else,” Sabàto told MSNBC from the convention floor. “I think Trump should just win it now and we can just move on and get our country back on track.” The actor ran for Congress in 2018, losing in a safe Democratic district. Madsen is best known for her work in the 2004 movie “Sideways” which garnered her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination.

articles.title: 'Daddy, I couldn't see anything': In 2009, 12-year-old Bahia Bakari was the only survivor when a Yemenia plane carrying 153 people crashed into the Indian Ocean; she could barely swim but clung to wreckage for about 13 hours until rescuers arrived
articles.summary: In June 2009, a 12-year-old girl who could barely swim found herself alone in the dark waters of the Indian Ocean after a passenger aircraft plunged into
articles.body: In June 2009, a 12-year-old girl who could barely swim found herself alone in the dark waters of the Indian Ocean after a passenger aircraft plunged into the sea near the Comoros Islands. Bahia Bakari clung to a piece of floating wreckage as rescuers searched for survivors. She was eventually pulled from the water by a sailor who jumped into the rough sea to reach her. According to an Associated Press report published at the time, French officials said she had been afloat for about 13 hours. She was the only survivor of the crash that killed 152 people, including her mother.The aircraft was Yemenia Airways Flight IY626, an Airbus A310-324 travelling from Sana’a in Yemen to Moroni, the capital of the Comoros. The flight was part of a longer journey that had originated in Paris, with stops in Marseille and Sana’a. It was carrying 142 passengers and 11 crew members, according to France’s Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety (BEA).The aircraft crashed into the sea during its approach to Moroni in the early hours of June 30, 2009. The BEA said air traffic controllers lost radio contact with the crew shortly before the aircraft struck the water, about 18 km from the airport. The accident occurred during a night-time approach in difficult weather conditions.A child thrown into the seaBahia had been travelling with her mother, Aziza Aboudou, to visit relatives in the Comoros. Her father, Kassim Bakari, was waiting in France with their other children. In the hours after the crash, he spoke to reporters about his daughter's limited swimming ability and the shock of learning that she had survived.In an interview with French radio, he recounted what Bahia had told him after she found herself in the water. Recalling what his daughter told him, her father, told The Guardian: “I asked her what happened and she said: ‘We saw the plane fall in the water. I found myself in the water. I was hearing people speak but I couldn't see anyone. I was in the dark. I couldn't see anything. Daddy, I couldn't swim very well. I grabbed on to something but I don't know what.’” Her father described her as a timid and fragile child who could barely swim. The fact that she had managed to remain afloat for hours made her survival even more extraordinary.Bahia later recalled that the aircraft had begun shaking shortly before the crash. In an interview published by the London Evening Standard in April 2012, she described sitting beside her mother, who was tired, as other passengers prepared for the landing. She remembered seeing the plane shake and being told to fasten her seat belt.After the impact, she found herself in the ocean, separated from her mother. She heard women crying and pleading for help nearby but could not see them or reach them. She tried to move towards the voices but struggled against the waves and exhaustion.The rescue at seaThe search for survivors was complicated by rough weather. According to an Associated Press account, the crew of a vessel searching the area encountered winds and waves reportedly reaching 16 feet. They eventually spotted Bahia clinging to a piece of debris. A member of the rescue team threw a life preserver towards her, but she was too exhausted and the sea was too rough for her to catch it. One of the sailors, Libouna Maturaffe Soulemane, then jumped into the water carrying a flotation device and reached her. The two were pulled aboard the rescue vessel, the Sima Com 2.The crew wrapped Bahia in blankets and gave her a warm drink. She was suffering from hypothermia and had sustained a fractured collarbone, along with bruises and other injuries. Despite the ordeal, she was conscious when rescuers brought her to safety.The rescue was followed by an emotional reunion with her father. Bahia was flown back to France on a government aircraft accompanied by officials, arriving at Le Bourget airport near Paris on July 2.The moment she learnt she was the only survivorFor a time, Bahia did not fully understand the scale of the disaster. She had heard other people in the water and continued to hope that her mother would be found. In her 2012 interview, she recalled that a hospital psychologist eventually told her that her mother was not coming back and that she was the sole survivor. It was only then that she understood what had happened to the people travelling with her.The crash prompted an international investigation involving authorities from the Comoros, France, Yemen and the United States. The BEA's investigation records the aircraft's registration, passenger and crew numbers, the loss of contact with air traffic control and the circumstances of the approach. articles.title: In 1944, a US Navy sailor rescued a kitten from Noumea Harbour in New Caledonia; aboard USS North Carolina, George received a service number and a health card listing him as Catholic
articles.summary: In 1944, Navy sailor Edward F. Cope rescued a kitten named George from New Caledonia. Aboard USS North Carolina, George was given a service number and health card, earning a unique place in naval history as an unofficial mascot.
articles.body: George the cat did not choose the Navy. As stated by The News & Observer and the August 2024 issue of the South Pacific WWII Museum, Edward F. Cope of the USS North Carolina rescued a kitten from Noumea Harbour in New Caledonia in 1944. By September, he had the kitten living in the lighting department aboard the USS North Carolina with official documentation. According to the South Pacific WWII Museum newsletter, the crew took the joke far enough to give the kitten a service number, a Navy health card picture and a religion: Catholic.Edward Cope rescued George at Noumea in August 1944According to the South Pacific WWII Museum’s newsletter, George arrived on the ship in August 1944. Cole & Marmalade quotes Cope as saying the ship’s photographer made up a liberty card for George and that the cat left the ship for good when it reached Seattle. The memorabilia belongs to Cope’s collection and his granddaughter, Vicky Knopf, carried it onto the ship during a visit some years ago. George had come to board a ship with a history. According to NCpedia, the USS North Carolina participated in every major offensive in the South Pacific over 40 months, carried 1,800 officers and sailors and earned 15 battle stars.George’s health card listed him as Catholic, with green eyes in peachy conditionFrom the newsletter, it is stated that George was enlisted by the crew as an electrician’s mate with a service number and his photo in the Navy health card. The health card gave George’s religion as being a Catholic, while his next of kin was the lighting shop crew. It was also stated that his eyes were green and healthy. The newsletter also gave the date of one physical examination of George as September 1944. According to Cole & Marmalade, the taunts were further developed as follows: the section on skin and glands was made fun of. They also drew the face of a cat on the anatomy diagram of a human and decided he was not entirely human in appearance or behaviour.Cats were never official Navy equipment and stress relief was the real jobThe National WWII Museum points out that cats had no official role like horses, dogs or mules. They were even allowed on board for rat prevention purposes in order to protect food supplies from diseases and to prevent rats from damaging the ropes and wires. According to its article, stress relief and some enjoyment were the primary role of all mascots and sometimes the crew adopted stray cats or kittens. Its newsletter stated that according to the creator of the ship, Mary Ames Booker, there have been animal mascots on ships called North Carolina since the early 1900s.USS Iowa’s dog Vicky had his own service record with number 000-00-00George was not the only animal with paperwork. In Naval History’s Paws of the Past, according to Dave Way and Captain Rich Abele, Vicky is the name of a dog that enlisted on November 11, 1942 and boarded the battleship USS Iowa on March 17, 1943. The service number on his ID was 000-00-00, with paw prints recorded in his file.The mood effect of an animal on a crew is hard to measure from 1944 records, but new research has looked at animals and service members directly. In a non-randomised control trial published in JAMA Network Open, researchers compared trained service dogs against usual care for 156 military members and veterans with PTSD. The National Institute of Child Health and Human Development described the research as the largest nationwide study to compare service-dog partnerships with usual care alone.After three months, participants who received service dogs reported lower PTSD symptom severity, anxiety and depression than the 75 participants in the control group. They also reported less social isolation and greater companionship. The study found an association between service dog partnerships and these improvements. As the mentioned test was conducted on trained service dogs used for post-9/11 veterans with PTSD, it does not provide any information concerning a ship’s cat in 1944.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bessent’s relocation: From US to EU, is Iran bringing war to Western soil?
articles.summary: A deliberate expansion of Iran’s campaign of retaliation beyond the Middle East could be taking place, said an expert.
articles.body:
The photograph was fairly grainy and devoid of much colour, but it was enough to make an impact. After the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) published an aerial view of US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s mansion in Georgetown in Washington, DC, it was capable of being geolocated.

“Iranian threats” against Bessent increased following the WSJ story in January 2025, which led to him being relocated to a United States military base for his safety, an anonymous source close to the matter told the Reuters news agency.

The New York Times first reported the move on Tuesday, citing three sources.

Bessent’s relocation is one of many similar moves made by US officials in recent years. The United Kingdom is also facing security threats it says are tied to Iran.

“I think we are witnessing a deliberate expansion of Iran’s campaign of retaliation beyond the Middle East,” Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera.

What happened to US Treasury Secretary Bessent?

Bessent has relocated from his Washington, DC mansion to a US military base following alleged Iranian threats to his life.

“The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran’s economy,” a US Treasury spokesperson said in an emailed statement to Reuters.

Of the WSJ report, an anonymous source told Reuters: “The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials.”

Bessent joins at least six other US officials who have left their Washington-area residences for a military base or other protected housing last year, including Stephen Miller , now the White House chief of staff, and Pam Bondi, then the attorney general, the New York Times reported.

Bessent has spearheaded US sanctions and the economic pressure campaign against Iran, dubbed Operation Economic Outcast , since August to coerce Tehran to end attacks on shipping and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28.

Threats have also been growing in the UK.

On Tuesday, the US military said it moved aircraft from a second ⁠airbase in the UK “in the wake of a threat from Iran”, WSJ reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Two US refuelling tankers and several other tankers that were using the Royal Air Force (RAF) Mildenhall military base in eastern England diverted to Germany and other locations on Monday, the outlet said.

The report comes weeks after five men were arrested outside the RAF Fairford airbase in southwest England over a security incident, with two others arrested later on suspicion of assisting Iranian intelligence.

In September, a British bomb disposal robot roamed the area near RAF Fairford, and 85 homes were evacuated amid fears of an attack.

Days later, the US sent B-1 bombers stationed there, which were used to strike Iran in its ongoing war, back home. About a dozen had been kept at the airbase.

On Wednesday, the US charged three men suspected in the plot to target the airbase. They are accused of acting in support of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Iraq’s Kataib Hezbollah.

While Tehran’s ambassador to the UK denied accusations that it was involved in ‌any ‌scheme against RAF, the IRGC in July had said that Fairford and any other base used to launch attacks against Iran were legitimate targets.

“Tehran increasingly regards American military facilities in Europe as part of the infrastructure sustaining the war against Iran,” said Kreig. “From that standpoint, [British airbases] are not peripheral to the conflict. They are integral to America’s ability to project military power against Iran.”

Analysts have previously told Al Jazeera the withdrawal of the US fleet from the UK reduced Washington’s ability to rapidly generate and sustain bombing missions.

What the episode highlighted, experts said, was the vulnerability of the US’s alliances and overseas basing in the face of potential threats by Iran.

What other threats does the US say it has faced?

In the US, officials claim that Iran’s ability to carry out large-scale attacks on its territory is limited.

However, last month Reuters reported that a senior intelligence official in the administration of US President Donald Trump warned in a memo that Iranian plots against US personnel and American citizens had reached an advanced stage.

Pointedly, the three men arrested on Tuesday for their alleged involvement in the RAF incident had played a role in nearly 20 attacks across the US and Europe, US prosecutors said.

The alleged assassination attempt against Trump during the campaign trail in 2024 marked another high-profile incident.

Iran rejected accusations that it was trying to kill Trump that year, shortly after a gunman opened fire at a rally in Pennsylvania, killing one person and wounding the then-presidential contender.

Iran has repeatedly denied plotting to attack officials and people on US soil.

Does Tehran have actual operational military capabilities outside the Middle East?

While the US and UK do not face the threat of an imminent attack by Iran, Tehran has demonstrated its “considerable reach” through the IRGC, Iraqi militias such as Kataib Hezbollah , and layered networks of local surrogates, argued Krieg.

“But its ability to conduct sophisticated attacks against heavily defended military installations … remains limited,” he said.

Still, Iran does not need sophisticated military capabilities to achieve strategic effects, said the analyst.

“Its intelligence services can mobilise networks of opportunity, involving ideologically motivated individuals, criminals and coincidental surrogates who may be recruited through payments rather than political allegiance,” said Krieg.

“Tehran wants to export the costs of the war to countries supporting Washington,” he explained. “If Iranian threats force American aircraft to disperse, increase security expenditure and generate political anxiety in Britain, Iran has already achieved something without firing a shot.”

So while a devastating military attack is improbable, said Krieg, “relatively modest acts of sabotage, combined with credible threats and psychological pressure, can impose disproportionate costs”.
