articles.title: Israel is ‘disrupting entire ecosystems’, including Lebanon’s wheat crop
articles.summary: Lebanese wheat production hit by war as farmlands face severe destruction in the south and Bekaa Valley.
articles.body:
Israel’s war on Lebanon has damaged the country’s wheat production and harmed the lives of farmers, experts told Al Jazeera.

For the last three years, Israel has been waging a war on Lebanon, where it has occupied large parts of the south and destroyed homes and infrastructure , in what some experts have said is a deliberate effort to make the land uninhabitable.

Repeated Israeli attacks have created havoc on the country’s wheat production, particularly in the south and in eastern Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley, where lands abandoned due to the impacts of war have increased to around 24 percent.

“They’re disrupting entire ecosystems,” Munira Khayyat, author of A Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “[Israel is] advancing the possibilities of drought and desertification, basically weakening the capacity of this land to hold life.”

Since 2023, Israel has been attacking large swaths of southern Lebanon, including using chemicals like white phosphorus, in what analysts and locals said was an effort to make the ground sterile or uninhabitable . A ceasefire was brokered in 2024 by France and the United States, but Israel never stopped attacking targets in Lebanon.

On March 2, Israel escalated its war on Lebanon for the second time in under two years. Hezbollah had attacked Israel following Israel’s assassination of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei two days earlier. The group also said it was in response to near-daily ceasefire violations by Israel.

Since then, Israel has reinvaded southern Lebanon, taking land up to 10 kilometres (6.2 miles) inside the country. Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-brokered framework agreement in June, which was supposed to put into motion so-called “pilot zones”. Under these pilot zones, Israeli troops would withdraw to be replaced by the Lebanese Armed Forces, who would also work to disarm Hezbollah.

Instead, Israeli troops have continued to level destruction in southern Lebanon, detonating homes and crucial infrastructure, including farmland.

“The South [of Lebanon] experienced the highest average losses [in wheat-growing areas], reaching 47 percent in 2023-2024 and 61 percent in 2024-2025,” Mariam Ibrahim, a researcher with Lebanon’s National Council for Scientific Research [CNRS-L] and author of a recent paper called “Wheat in Crisis” that tracked Lebanon’s wheat struggles from 2017 to 2025, told Al Jazeera. “The Bekaa plain, which accounts for approximately 64 percent of Lebanon’s national wheat production, was also significantly affected, losing around 43 percent and 57 percent of its wheat area during the two respective seasons.”

In areas like the border town Bint Jbeil , 100 percent of cropland was destroyed, while in the Baalbeck district to the east, the study says approximately 32 percent of cropland was destroyed.

Ibrahim said the Russian-Ukrainian war led to an increase in bread prices and incentivised some domestic Lebanese production.

“The depreciation of the Lebanese pound meant that farmers could potentially generate higher revenues and profits in local currency when selling their wheat, as wheat prices were increasingly influenced by international market prices,” she said. “This provided an additional economic incentive to expand wheat cultivation, and our results showed that Lebanon’s wheat cultivation area reached its peak [during] the 2022-2023 season.”

However, experts said that since 2023, Israel’s war on Lebanon led to the proportion of land that had been used to grow wheat that was now left fallow increasing from 9 percent to 24 percent, mostly in the south and the Bekaa Valley.

Elias Ghadban, a food security expert with the independent Beirut-based consultancy firm AgriDev, told Al Jazeera that the destruction of land used to farm wheat has not made a “significant difference” at the national level, but it has had a damaging effect on southern wheat farmers who “lost their livelihoods”.

Ghadban also pointed to the fact that the cost of living has increased in Lebanon while salaries have failed to match that increase. “The expenditure on basic needs went up,” he said.

The economic crisis, followed by three years of war, has devastated many farmers, particularly as much of southern Lebanon’s farmland is largely unindustrialised. Experts warn that the destruction caused by Israel’s war could prevent many farmers from rebuilding their livelihoods, even after the fighting ends.

“All those small farmers who have made southern Lebanon what it is today and have been able to hold that land through their attachment to it, through their farming of it, through their existential need to be on that land in order to make their lives viable, that’s going to be broken,” Khayyat said.

articles.title: ‘It’s just too expensive’: Housing and wages at the heart of Spain’s strike
articles.summary: Mass walkout across several cities marks first general strike in 14 years.
articles.body:
Madrid, Spain – In central Madrid, business owners seemed to have taken note of the riots that erupted in Paris last month.

Amid a nationwide strike , many have boarded up their shop windows on Wednesday.

Police are lined up in front of some major department stores. At others, police vans protect the entrances.

This is the first national general strike in Spain in 14 years, and it is all about the lack of affordable housing .

The protesters who have blocked the city’s central Gran Via are angry and frustrated.

The catalyst for the strike was the eviction, in September, of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal , known as Maricarmen, from her home of seventy years because she could not afford a fivefold increase in her monthly rent of 500 euros ($555).

It exposed a crisis in the lack of affordable housing, particularly in the country’s major cities.

“Housing is a fundamental problem”, Antonio, a teacher, tells us. “It consumes the majority of a working person’s wages. Wages – or rather, the need for wage increases – are another fundamental issue. We are fighting for a combination of things: lower housing costs and higher wages.”

The country’s youth council says that a young person would need to spend 98.7 percent of their monthly salary to rent a place on their own.

Arturo, who is in his mid-30s, says he cannot afford a place of his own. “It’s just too expensive, so I’m living with my parents.

“Once you factor in the cost of food and basic living expenses, you’re left with almost nothing – maybe 100 euros [$110]. And that’s just not … sustainable in the long run.”

Madrid’s teachers have been on strike since the start of term.

Antonio teaches in one of the city’s schools.

“I am deeply concerned about the social rights of my students, their families, and my neighbours,” he says. “I believe that all citizens need to have a social consciousness: if things aren’t going well for everyone, then they can’t go well for any of us. It is absolutely essential that we all stand up and fight for everyone’s rights.”

The Bank of Spain says 750,000 new homes are needed to meet current demand, and that could rise to a million. In 2025, 92,000 homes were built.

The housing crisis could end up costing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez his job.

The snap general election he called will take place on November 29, after his minority government failed to get legislation through parliament that would have given some protections to tenants.

Sanchez’s Socialist Party is trailing in the polls behind the combined support for right-wing and far-right parties.

articles.title: A Louisiana man's 2015 will left his property to his wife, excluding children from another relationship; after six of his nine children got the will voided, an appeals court reversed that ruling in November 2026
articles.summary: A Louisiana appeals court has restored the validity of a man's 2015 will, which left all his property to his wife.
articles.body: A Louisiana appeals court has restored the validity of a man's 2015 will, which left all his property to his wife. The court reversed a lower court ruling that had declared the will invalid after six of his nine children challenged it. The judgment was delivered by the Louisiana Court of Appeal, First Circuit, on November 6.Louis Edward Lloyd Sr. died in 2021, leaving behind his wife, Evelyn Robertson Lloyd, and nine children. Three children were born from his marriage to Evelyn, while the other six were from a different relationship.According to the judgement, in his will, he wrote in 2015, Lloyd left all his property, including his separate and community property, to Evelyn. She approached the court in December 2021, seeking recognition as the sole legatee and possession of his estate. The trial court accepted her request and issued a judgment recognising her as the sole legatee.However, six of Lloyd's children challenged the decision in October 2022, seeking to annul the will and reopen the succession proceedings.Six children questioned the will's validityThe children initially argued that the will was invalid because Louis E. Lloyd Jr. was totally disabled and qualified as a forced heir under Louisiana law.They also questioned the signatures on the document. Lloyd's name appeared in printed form on the first page but in cursive on the second. The children argued that this difference raised doubts about whether the will had been properly signed.In July 2024, the trial court declared Louis E. Lloyd Jr. a forced heir. The children later filed another motion in January 2025, seeking to have the will declared an absolute nullity.They argued that the document did not meet the legal requirements for a notarial testament. They also questioned whether it was the same document executed before the notary.Evelyn opposed the challenge, arguing that the children had to prove the will was invalid. However, on April 3, 2025, the trial court accepted their arguments and annulled the will. After her request for a new trial was rejected, Evelyn appealed.Revised Louisiana law became relevantWhile the appeal was pending, Louisiana revised its rules governing notarial wills through Act 30 of 2025, which came into effect on August 1, 2025.Under the earlier rules, a testator who could read and sign had to sign at the end of the will and on every separate page. The notary and two witnesses also had to sign a declaration confirming its execution.The revised law removed the requirement that the testator sign every page. It stated that the signature could appear anywhere in the document, provided it identified the testator and showed an intention to adopt it as their will.The changes applied retrospectively to pending cases. Since the dispute had not been finally decided when the law took effect, the appeals court said the revised requirements applied to Lloyd's will.Court says children failed to prove invalidityThe appeals court examined the will and the deposition of Linda E. Hodge, the notary who prepared it. Hodge testified that Lloyd had read the document and signed it in front of two witnesses, Marsha Strickland and Eugene Hodge Sr.She also identified another document carrying a "True Copy" stamp. It contained typographical errors, including an incorrect name for one of Lloyd's children. However, Hodge could not clearly recall why it had been stamped or all the circumstances surrounding its preparation.The judges found that the will appeared to meet the revised legal requirements. It was written, dated and executed before a notary in the presence of two witnesses. It also carried the signatures of Lloyd, the witnesses and the notary.The court said Louisiana law presumes that a testament is valid. The responsibility to prove otherwise rested with the children who sought to annul it.The judges found that they had failed to establish that Lloyd had not signed or dated the document or that it had not been properly executed. The existence of another version did not, by itself, prove that the will was invalid.The appeals court reversed the August 12, 2026 amended judgment that had annulled the will. It sent the case back to the trial court for further proceedings and ordered the six children to pay the costs of the appeal.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is reportedly attempting to regain her position, following a brief tenure that ended amid criticism. Sources suggest she is seeking support from Trump and his new chief of staff, Stephen Miller.
articles.body: Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is reportedly seeking another opportunity to take up the position after her brief five-day tenure ended last month, with sources close to US President Donald Trump claiming she has been trying to regain his support.Three people familiar with the matter told The New York Post that Zacharia has been attempting to build favour with Trump and his newly appointed chief of staff, Stephen Miller. At the same time, the administration considers changes to its communications team.One source told the publication that Zacharia believed her appearance on Right Side Broadcasting Network (RSBN) during election-night coverage on Tuesday could help her make a case for returning to the White House podium.“She said it out loud,” the source said, describing her reported plan as “absurd” and “truly embarrassing”.However, another person who spoke with Zacharia this week said she later claimed the remark about using the television appearance to secure her former position had been made as a joke.Zacharia was also seen at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida over the weekend, as the President prepared for further changes within his administration. One person who observed her at the resort's patio on Saturday claimed she was trying to attract Trump's attention.“She will never go back. [Trump] thinks she's a joke. She has zero chance of that,” the source told NYP, adding that the President had described her as a “train wreck”.A White House official also dismissed the possibility of her return, saying: “She never stopped. She's psychotic. She thinks she did a good job at her one briefing.”Zacharia denies seeking another White House roleDespite the claims about her efforts to return, people close to Zacharia have disputed the suggestion that she wants the press secretary position again.A source close to the former press secretary told The New York Post that she was not interested in reclaiming the role and was instead “focused on defending free speech and supporting the president's priorities through other mediums”.Another person familiar with her position was equally emphatic, saying: “I am 1,000% certain Katie Zacharia has no interest in going and being the press secretary at the White House.”Zacharia has also publicly praised Miller and his role in leading the Trump administration's mass deportation campaign. Her comments have added to speculation about her relationship with the new chief of staff, although the report does not establish that Miller is supporting her return.5-day tenure ended after brief White House briefingZacharia's previous appointment lasted only five days. Her sole White House press briefing lasted 14 minutes, during which she reportedly struggled to handle the session.She also faced criticism following appearances on Fox News programmes hosted by Sean Hannity and Fox & Friends.According to NYP, some White House aides were particularly unhappy with her comments to Hannity, in which she suggested that her performance during the briefing had been affected by inadequate preparation from subordinates.The remarks reportedly angered colleagues within the administration. One White House official dismissed the prospect of her returning, saying it would not happen in “a million years”.Caroline Sunshine also linked to vacant positionZacharia is not the only person reportedly being considered for the vacant press secretary position.Caroline Sunshine, a former Disney Channel actress who previously worked in Trump's first administration, has also emerged as a possible contender.A source told the newspaper that Sunshine had been attempting to arrange meetings with Trump as she sought consideration for the role.The press secretary position remains vacant following Zacharia's departure. Trump has also recently replaced Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with Miller, marking a major personnel change after Republicans suffered significant losses in the midterm elections.The reports of Zacharia's possible return have been met with scepticism among administration officials. One official joked about the prospect, saying: “I've given birth without drugs and I still can't imagine that level of pain tolerance.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: High school recruit flips commitment from Colorado to Mississippi State back to Colorado in 30-hour span
articles.summary: Li'Marcus Jones, a top Nashville offensive tackle, flipped from Colorado to Mississippi State only to reverse course back to the Buffs within 30 hours.
articles.body: Stop me if you've heard this before, but college football recruiting is not for the faint of heart. I mentioned it yesterday, but this is a 365-day-a-year racket, and if coaches don't stay on top of things in the talent acquisition world, they'll be run out of town so fast it will make your head spin. Recruiting is the lifeblood of every great program, but unfortunately, a lot of the inner workings of acquiring high school talent is getting on a plane every weekend and telling a bunch of 16- and 17-year-olds how great they are, only to see them choose another school in the 11th hour because they offered their grandma a house or something. It's a thankless job, and oftentimes the antics of some of these high school athletes will be enough to make you want to stop watching college football altogether. Take Li'Marcus Jones, for example (great name, by the way). Jones is an offensive tackle from the Nashville area and one of the top recruits in the state of Tennessee. For a while, he was verbally committed to the University of Colorado. COLLEGE FOOTBALL COACHING CAROUSEL COULD EXPLODE AS LINCOLN RILEY AND DEION SANDERS FACE MOUNTING PRESSURE With how the season is going for coach Prime and the Buffs, though, it was only a matter of time before some of their committed prospects started to look elsewhere, and Jones apparently decided to finally pull the plug and stay a little closer to home, opting to flip to Mississippi State on Monday afternoon. Seems like a solid choice, given the Bulldogs' success early in the season when quarterback Kamario Taylor and running back Fluff Bothwell were still healthy. It is a program on the rise, especially on offense, and I'm sure any lineman would be more than happy to block for those two guys. But just as it seemed Li'Marcus found his home for the next four years (or at least until the transfer portal opened next winter), it happened. 30 hours. That's all it took for Jones to get cold feet and flip back to Colorado. You would think someone would tell this kid, "Hey, take a day or two to think this over before doing something rash." Or, at the very least, hand him a dictionary so he can look up the word "commitment." I'm not trying to pick on Li'Marcus here, because plenty of recruits do stuff like this. Hell, he's not even the first one to do it this recruiting cycle. Oddly enough, this happened back in June, also involving Colorado and a school from the Magnolia State (Ole Miss). articles.title: Ole Miss students ‘devastated’ by racist monkey gestures and noises captured on door camera
articles.summary: One of the women caught on camera making monkey noises and gestures at the apartment door of three Black Ole Miss students doubled down when confronted at the time, a woman who lives in the home told “CBS Morning.”
articles.body: One of the women caught on camera making monkey noises and gestures at the apartment door of three Black Ole Miss students doubled down when confronted at the time, a woman who lives in the home told “CBS Morning.” The video shows three women, who appear to be white, walking by the front door of the off-campus apartment where the three Black students live Friday. One is seen beating her chest. She and the second woman are seen and heard making ape noises. The third woman in the video walks by the door without stopping. Jakiyra Metcalf and Victoria Johnson live in the apartment, and Metcalf said she and Johnson went outside to confront the women shortly after seeing the video on their doorbell. Johnson said in Wednesday’s “CBS Morning” interview that one of the women, later identified as Alaina Kunes, 18, apologized when they stepped outside to speak with her. Kunes told her and Metcalf they had done the same at four doors, adding, “We didn’t mean any harm,” Johnson said, adding that she did not see them target any other doors. However, Johnson said the second woman, who has not been identified and has not commented on the incident, doubled down when confronted. “She continued to make the gestures after the girl was apologizing. It was like a slap in the face,” Johnson told CBS. Kunes apologized Tuesday for the racist gestures, saying she recognized her actions “were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful.” She also said she was “unaware” of the women’s race until the video gained national attention and said she hoped for the apartment residents’ forgiveness. The three women living in the apartment told CBS that they were left “hurt and devastated” by the racist mockery and that it was “very disheartening.” Asked whether they could forgive Kunes, Metcalf said that whether or not Kunes knew her and her roommates’ race, the gesture and noises were “very disrespectful.” “I just have mixed feelings about it,” Metcalf said. Metcalf’s roommate Kaiyden Caldwell said she appreciates the apology, “but I feel like it still doesn’t change what happened on that Friday because it’s still hurtful and it’s still devastating that someone would come to our camera and do that.” Kunes has withdrawn from the university, a source close to her told NBC News. The status of the other women is unknown. After the incident, Johnson said she wants people “to be mindful of their actions” and for others in similar situations to speak out instead of sweeping things under the rug. “This is a reality for us and I feel like voices need to be heard,” she said. Mississippi University said in an email to students Sunday that it has launched an investigation.

articles.title: Israel's political shake-up enters new phase as former PM plays kingmaker — and deadline looms
articles.summary: Benjamin Netanyahu called for unity, but Gadi Eisenkot canceled Likud talks after calling the outgoing prime minister's speech "delusional."
articles.body: Israel's newly elected parliament was sworn in Tuesday, marking the beginning of a political transition that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long tenure in power. Despite the opposition's parliamentary gains, the country remains without a new government, and negotiations to form one face significant obstacles. At the center of those negotiations is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who was tasked by President Isaac Herzog on Sunday with assembling Israel's next governing coalition after 67 lawmakers recommended him for the position, compared with 46 who supported Netanyahu. Although Eisenkot's Yashar party won 21 seats in the Oct. 27 election, he is working closely with former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, whose B'Yachad party, formed with former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, secured another 12 seats. NETANYAHU FACES COALITION SHOWDOWN AS RIVALS MANEUVER TO FORM ISRAEL'S NEXT GOVERNMENT The two parties have not merged, but their cooperation effectively gives Eisenkot the negotiating backing of 33 lawmakers — more than Netanyahu's Likud, which remains the largest individual party in the Knesset with 27 seats. A source with knowledge of discussions within the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu told Fox News Digital that Bennett has decided to act as a political kingmaker, supporting Eisenkot's leadership bid rather than seeking the premiership himself. Bennett intends to coordinate closely with Eisenkot throughout the negotiations while preserving his party's independent leadership and parliamentary identity, according to the source. The arrangement does not create a new 33-seat party or guarantee that the two leaders will agree on every coalition arrangement. But it places Eisenkot in a stronger negotiating position than his party's 21 seats alone would suggest. During Tuesday's swearing-in of the new Knesset, Netanyahu called for a national unity government, citing Israel's security challenges, but also sharply attacked the Arab parties, accusing them of supporting terrorism and warning against forming a government dependent on their votes. Bennett, normally an outspoken political figure who has largely avoided the spotlight during the coalition negotiations, broke his relative silence to repeatedly confront Netanyahu during the speech. FORMER ISRAELI PM EMERGES AS WILD CARD IN HIGH-STAKES ELECTION WITH MIDDLE EAST'S FUTURE AT STAKE "What about your Qatari advisors?" Bennett shouted, referring to the investigation into allegations that members of Netanyahu's inner circle had financial ties to Qatar while working for the prime minister. Bennett also demanded to know why Netanyahu had not established a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and challenged him to declare Qatar an enemy state. The confrontation disrupted Netanyahu's address, with other lawmakers joining the shouting as the prime minister continued warning against a government supported by Arab parties. Eisenkot responded with an unusually forceful condemnation. "I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister’s delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech," Eisenkot said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital on Nov. 10. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute." Eisenkot subsequently instructed his negotiating team to cancel a meeting scheduled with Likud representatives for Wednesday. In a separate statement, Yashar said the canceled meeting had been intended to explore coalition possibilities based on Eisenkot's four governing principles, but Netanyahu's speech made the planned discussions untenable. FORMER ISRAELI ARMY CHIEF GADI EISENKOT EMERGES AS NETANYAHU’S LEADING ELECTION CHALLENGER Netanyahu, however, continued advocating for a unity government on Wednesday, arguing that Israel's security challenges demanded cooperation across political divisions, according to The Times of Israel. Despite the public confrontation, a national unity government remains one of the most tangible scenarios under consideration, according to a source with knowledge of negotiations within the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu. The source told Fox News Digital that such an arrangement would depend on Netanyahu agreeing not to serve as prime minister first, potentially allowing Eisenkot to lead the government under a rotation agreement while Netanyahu assumes the position of alternate prime minister. Eisenkot's allies are keeping several options open, according to the source, including agreements with ultra-Orthodox or Arab parties, partly to strengthen their negotiating position and increase pressure on Netanyahu to accept a power-sharing arrangement. But whether Netanyahu would agree to relinquish the premiership, even temporarily, remains unclear. The source emphasized that negotiations are fluid and that no agreement has been reached. NETANYAHU GAINS OVERNIGHT AS ISRAEL ELECTION HEADS TOWARD POLITICAL DEADLOCK Why forming a government remains so complicated The official election results left Netanyahu's bloc with 53 seats, while the four parties seeking to replace him secured 48. The remaining 19 seats went to two Arab-led parties: the Joint List, with 11, and Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, with eight. While 67 lawmakers supported Eisenkot receiving the mandate to form a government, that support does not automatically translate into a workable governing coalition. Herzog acknowledged the challenge during consultations with parliamentary leaders, citing disagreements and mutual political vetoes that could prevent either side from forming a stable government. Eisenkot's principal partners are Bennett, Lapid, Yair Golan of the Democrats and Avigdor Liberman of Yisrael Beytenu. Together, their parties hold 48 seats, 13 short of the 61 generally needed for a parliamentary majority. Eisenkot has outlined four principles for potential coalition partners: recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence, supporting military or civilian national service for all, and recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization whose military and governing capabilities must be dismantled. But those conditions have created a difficult political equation. The ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, collectively hold 13 seats — precisely the number Eisenkot's existing four-party bloc would need to reach 61. However, both parties have historically opposed broadening military conscription to include ultra-Orthodox religious students, directly conflicting with Eisenkot's demand for national service. At a Nov. 10 faction meeting, Eisenkot reiterated that he would not abandon the principle of universal military, national or civilian service, according to The Times of Israel. The disagreement became even more visible Wednesday, when Bennett's party submitted legislation proposing expanded benefits for soldiers and reservists, while United Torah Judaism introduced bills seeking to preserve military draft exemptions for religious students, The Times of Israel reported Tuesday. The Arab parties present a different challenge. While Ra'am's eight lawmakers could help Eisenkot establish a government, Liberman has rejected relying on Arab parties, and the political acceptability of such an arrangement remains disputed within the bloc. A source within Eisenkot's party told Fox News Digital that the party has not categorically ruled out cooperation with Ra'am, provided its leadership accepts the four governing principles. The source acknowledged that negotiations remain difficult and that multiple coalition arrangements are still under consideration. One option involves securing the support of ultra-Orthodox parties. Another would require cooperation with Arab lawmakers, potentially including support from outside the government. A broader national unity arrangement involving Likud has also been discussed. Each scenario presents political obstacles, leaving Eisenkot facing the difficult task of assembling a coalition among parties with sharply different views on religion, national identity and security policy. NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE Eisenkot moves to challenge Netanyahu before taking power Even without a new government, Eisenkot and his allies have begun exercising their influence in the newly sworn-in parliament. In a Monday statement provided to Fox News Digital, Yashar announced that it had submitted legislation to establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks and introduce term limits for the prime minister. The party also submitted proposals to repeal legislation associated with Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, including changes to the judiciary, the attorney general's authority, the police and the circumstances under which a prime minister can be declared unable to serve. A vote to replace current Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, is scheduled for Nov. 17. The appointments could give Eisenkot's allies considerable influence over Israel's legislative agenda before they secure control of the government. Eisenkot signals a different approach to Washington Beyond the domestic political negotiations, Eisenkot has also sought to reassure American leaders about the future of U.S.-Israel relations. In a Nov. 4 public statement addressed to Americans and the international community, Eisenkot pledged to restore bipartisan cooperation with Washington and deepen Israel's relationship with the United States. "The bond between Israel and the United States is more than an alliance between governments," Eisenkot wrote. "It is a partnership between peoples, built over generations, sustained by shared democratic values, and strengthened by the conviction that our nations are more secure and more prosperous when we stand together." He also directly addressed his willingness to work with President Donald Trump. "I look forward to working closely and constructively with President Trump and his administration, whose friendship and commitment to Israel we deeply value," Eisenkot said. The message comes amid heightened debate in Washington over the future of U.S. support for Israel, following the American midterm elections and disagreements over the country's regional policies. A source within Eisenkot's party told Fox News Digital that rebuilding relations with the United States, including with both major American political parties, would be among the priorities of a new government. Eisenkot has also emphasized his intention to pursue regional cooperation and diplomatic opportunities while maintaining Israel's security commitments. ISRAEL HEADS INTO DEEPLY DIVIDED ELECTION AS OCT. 7 RECKONING LOOMS: WHAT TO KNOW What happens next? Under Israeli law, Eisenkot has 28 days from Nov. 8 to form a government, giving him until Dec. 6 to reach an agreement. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 additional days, potentially pushing the deadline to Dec. 20. If Eisenkot fails, the president may give another lawmaker the opportunity to form a government. Additional parliamentary procedures would follow if a second attempt also fails, potentially culminating in another national election. The outcome could determine not only who becomes Israel's next prime minister, but also the country's direction on military conscription, judicial reform, accountability for October 7 and its relations with Washington. For now, Israel is experiencing an unusual political transition: a newly elected parliament is beginning to challenge the outgoing government's agenda, while the leader tasked with forming its replacement is still negotiating over who will join him. What he does not yet have is an agreement among those parties on how to govern together.

articles.title: Tens of thousands join Poland’s nationalist Independence Day march
articles.summary: Polish PM Donald Tusk calls for restraint, urging unity after deadly Krakow attack linked to far-right ideology.
articles.body:
Tens of thousands of nationalist sympathisers have gathered in Poland’s capital, Warsaw, for an Independence Day march, days after a mass shooting in Krakow killed six people.

Participants carrying Polish flags assembled in central Warsaw on Wednesday, as police officers were deployed at the scene to secure the demonstration.

The Independence Day march, which has long been a source of tension between right-wing groups and Poland’s governing centrists, has been held annually on November 11 since 1918 to commemorate the end of more than 100 years of partition by Russia, Prussia and Austria.

The annual march has faced criticism for anti-Semitic and anti-immigration rhetoric, while supporters say the gathering, held under the motto “A Pole is the host in Poland”, is an expression of national pride.

Organisers of the march said they expected a record turnout, with many foreign nationalists set to attend, including Spain’s Revuelta, a youth movement linked to Vox, and members of the Hungarian far-right Mi Hazank party.

Poland’s conservative-nationalist President Karol Nawrocki was seen attending the march and has previously participated in both his official capacity and as a private citizen.

Poland “does not exist today so that the political elites can grant themselves the right to manage citizens … against the will of the nation”, Nawrocki said, alluding to the centrist government.

Prior to the march, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk appealed for restraint amid heightened political divisions after ministers said the man who killed six people and wounded more than a dozen in the main square of Krakow on Saturday, November 7 may have been motivated by ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌far-right ideology.

“We may hold different views, we may keep each other in check, and at times we may even be political opponents,” Tusk said. “Anyone who truly cares about Poland must understand that this space, defined by independence, freedom and a secure Republic, is a common good.”

On Tuesday, Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek said the killer had been interested in the neo-Nazi Anders Behring Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.

On Monday, the police announced that the 24-year-old gunman died at a hospital after he was shot by police officers and arrested on Saturday when he opened fire from his car.
